meta.source: Cor v2 Supabase (anon REST, build-time read)

thesis: Human systems signal when their conditions are not met, and modern environments withhold those conditions at scale. Preferences are mechanism outputs, not ground truth. The load-bearing claim of every proxy gradient: the cue is identical at every level; only the resolving function changes, so a proxy can fire the cue without supplying what actually resolves it.

foundations.name: Fitness Interface
foundations.statement: Access to the world is mediated by evolved fitness interfaces, not guaranteed veridicality.
foundations.derivation: Hoffman (Interface Theory of Perception), Prakash et al. (Fitness Beats Truth theorem).

foundations.name: Signal-Default Epistemology
foundations.statement: Motivational-emotional outputs are treated as prima facie informative about the organism's regulated conditions, by default. The signal is read as information about input conditions and current state, not as noise to be suppressed. This is a diagnostic default, not a presumption of veridicality (OF1 stands). Reading the signal as information is no argument against relieving it. The default is displaced in two ways. A clear physical defect displaces it outright, whether a test has found it yet or not, and the output is then a symptom of that defect: acute organic disease or state shift (an infection or autoimmune disease, an endocrine disease such as a thyroid fault, delirium), structural damage, a large-effect genetic variant with measurable physical effects, and substance or medication effects. A setting left by deprivation far outside the evolved range (DA7) and chronic dysregulation displace the reading of the current input without making the output a disease: the output answers that setting, or a loop that keeps running, more than the present input. An ordinary hard childhood is no such setting: it explains little of how an adult feels (DA7). Sleep loss and low-grade inflammation that a mismatched life produces also displace the reading of the current input without making the output a disease. A marker that only shows sensitivity is no defect. Chronic dysregulation counts as a physical cause only where a clear defect is behind it, such as an infection or another separate disease.
foundations.derivation: Frame layer, sibling of OF1. Methodological commitment that follows from P2 + DA1 + DA7: if the architecture is domain-sensitive (P2), and aversive outputs are intelligible defensive signals (DA1), and the architecture calibrates to developmental input (DA7), then the default reading of any mechanism output must be accurate to the environment the mechanism was calibrated for. Decoupling is the exception requiring evidence.

foundations.name: Inclusive Fitness
foundations.statement: Inclusive fitness - survival and reproduction - is the loss function of selection, not of the organism's runtime computation.

foundations.name: Domain-Sensitive Interacting Adaptations
foundations.statement: The organism contains evolved, domain-sensitive, interacting functional adaptations.
foundations.derivation: Tooby & Cosmides (design principle), confirmed empirically by Panksepp, Bowlby, Dunbar, Boehm, Trivers, Gilbert, Rozin.

foundations.name: Systematic Mismatch
foundations.statement: Where modern environments depart from the conditions these adaptations evolved in, they push the adaptations outside their expected or regulatable operating ranges.
foundations.derivation: Eaton & Konner (discordance), Gluckman & Hanson (developmental mismatch), Li/van Vugt/Colarelli (mismatch review). Constrained by Boyd & Richerson / Henrich.

foundations.name: Defensive Signals Under Mismatch
foundations.statement: Where no clear physical defect is the cause, aversive outputs are intelligible defensive signals under mismatch, not evidence of defective design.
foundations.derivation: P2 + P3 + Nesse (negative outputs as defenses) + McEwen (reversible with environmental correction) + Birkett & Newton-Fisher (all 40 captive chimps studied showed abnormal behavior; none reported in wild observation).

foundations.name: Socially Scaffolded Regulation
foundations.statement: Human regulation is constitutively socially scaffolded; social context is the highest-leverage cross-cutting input dimension.
foundations.derivation: Dunbar + Coan & Sbarra (social baseline) + Bowlby (attachment) + Hrdy (cooperative breeding).

foundations.name: Recurrent Coupling and Cascading
foundations.statement: Systems are recurrently coupled; perturbations propagate and can self-maintain across domains.
foundations.derivation: Panksepp (cross-system inhibition) + Felitti (ACE dose-response) + Borsboom (network psychopathology) + McEwen (cumulative cross-system activation).

foundations.name: Proxy Hijacking via Open Loops
foundations.statement: Proxy cues can activate systems without meeting the conditions that normally regulate or terminate them.

foundations.name: Defensive Over-Activation Bias
foundations.statement: Defensive systems err toward over-activation under asymmetric error costs.
foundations.derivation: Haselton & Buss (error management) + Nesse (smoke detector) + P1.

foundations.name: Competing Motivational Programs
foundations.statement: The architecture contains partially competing motivational programs and tradeoff structures.
foundations.derivation: Trivers (parent-offspring conflict, reciprocal altruism) + Boehm (dominance + anti-dominance) + Gilbert (approach + submit).

foundations.name: Developmental Calibration
foundations.statement: The architecture calibrates to developmental and ongoing environmental input within evolved ranges.
foundations.derivation: Bowlby (internal working models) + Hrdy + McEwen + Meaney (HPA-axis calibration).

foundations.name: Phylogenetic Priority
foundations.statement: Motivational programs have phylogenetically determined priority relations. Older, survival-critical systems can suppress or commandeer newer systems.
foundations.derivation: Panksepp (phylogenetic depth of affective circuits) + cross-species conservation evidence.

foundations.name: Non-Substitutability of Mechanism Resolution
foundations.statement: Mechanism resolution conditions are not fully interchangeable. Improvement in one mechanism can buffer or modulate consequences in another, especially where mechanisms are recurrently coupled (DA3), but cross-system buffering does not generally replace the specific resolution conditions of an impaired mechanism. Well-being is often bottlenecked by severe unresolved deficits in individual mechanisms and is not well described as a simple average across mechanism states.
foundations.derivation: Follows from P2 (domain-sensitive interacting adaptations: if mechanisms are domain-sensitive, their resolution conditions are not freely interchangeable). Coupling and cross-system buffering effects are handled separately by DA3 (Recurrent Coupling and Cascading); DA9 specifically claims non-fungibility of resolution conditions, not absence of cross-system effects. Liebig's 1840 Law of the Minimum is the historical analogy for the bottleneck pattern.

foundations.name: Heritable Parameter Variation
foundations.statement: Architecture parameters (drive gains, thresholds, calibration setpoints) vary between individuals within heritable ranges.
foundations.derivation: Complements DA7: DA7 says the environment tunes the operating point, developmentally and ongoing; DA10 says the tunable ranges themselves differ per person, substantially heritably. Grounded by C15 triangulation across three independent method families: twin designs (Polderman et al. 2015 meta-analysis of fifty years of twin studies), adoption/family designs (Plomin program), and molecular SNP-heritability from unrelated individuals (Yang et al. 2010 GCTA line). Canonical framing: Turkheimer 2000 three laws of behavior genetics.

foundations.name: Allostatic Load Accumulation
foundations.statement: Chronic unresolved activation accumulates as allostatic load.

foundations.name: Market Proxy Exploitation
foundations.statement: Markets can industrialize proxy exploitation of unmet regulatory needs.
foundations.derivation: P3 + DA4 + market incentive structures + empirical (Moss food, Schull gambling, Haugen attention, Muldoon & Parke companion AI; children ate more after a single exposure to food adverts in the experiments pooled by Boyland et al. 2016).

foundations.name: Environment as Primary Intervention Layer
foundations.statement: Cortical override of subcortical activation is costly and tiring, and chronic defensive activation downregulates the cortical override machinery itself. Interventions that undo a mismatch, moving the organism's actual input conditions toward what it evolved for (the baseline rows of this atlas), are therefore more durable and less effort-dependent than interventions targeting cognitive override alone. The environment is a primary intervention layer for systemic and population-scale change, and is currently underweighted by major institutions.
foundations.derivation: Empirical corollary of DA8 (phylogenetic priority) + DA9 (non-fungibility of resolution conditions). DA8 + DA9 do not logically entail DC3 - they make environmental intervention a plausible higher-leverage path for systemic design, but the strength of the leverage is an empirical question. Supported by Sapolsky Forest Troop (N=1 troop, striking but limited generalization); Roseto Effect (observational, contested); Ilardi Therapeutic Lifestyle Change (author-reported response rates from a 2007 conference presentation and a 2009 trade book; no peer-reviewed RCT); BEIP foster care (single trial, large effect on reactive attachment disorder signs); captive-chimpanzee enrichment (variable but reproducible).

convergences.name: Threat-Detection via Ancient Subcortical Circuits
convergences.statement: Threat detection and defensive response are mediated by phylogenetically ancient subcortical circuits (amygdala, periaqueductal gray, hypothalamus) that operate pre-attentively and can override cortical processing - established independently by Panksepp's FEAR-system neuroanatomy, the Öhman/Mineka backward-masking fear-module research program, and Nesse's clinical evolutionary psychiatry linking panic and anxiety to these defensive systems.
independent_literatures: Öhman & Mineka fear module visual attention / backward masking
Nesse evolutionary psychiatry of panic and anxiety

convergences.name: Wanting-Liking Dissociation as Proxy Hijack
convergences.statement: Motivational pursuit ('wanting', mediated by mesolimbic dopamine) is dissociable from hedonic satisfaction ('liking'), creating an open-loop vulnerability where proxy cues can activate the SEEKING system without providing the conditions that normally terminate or resolve it - established independently by Berridge & Robinson's incentive-salience neuroscience, Tinbergen's supernormal-stimuli ethology, and Panksepp's SEEKING-circuit affective neuroscience.
independent_literatures: Berridge & Robinson incentive salience / mesolimbic dopamine

convergences.name: Socially Scaffolded Regulation via Attachment
convergences.statement: Human regulation is constitutively socially scaffolded: the organism's default expectation is proximity to trusted co-regulators, and this scaffolding is architectural rather than optional - established independently by Coan's Social Baseline Theory fMRI program, Bowlby's attachment theory, Hrdy's cooperative-breeding thesis, Dunbar's social-brain hypothesis, and Holt-Lunstad's mortality meta-analysis showing 50% survival advantage from strong social relationships.
independent_literatures: Coan social baseline theory affective neuroscience

convergences.name: Reciprocity, Norm Enforcement, and Coalition Architecture
convergences.statement: Humans have specialized architecture for reciprocal exchange, cheater detection, norm enforcement, and coalitional identity - supported independently by Fehr & Gächter's experimental altruistic-punishment findings, Boehm's reverse-dominance coalition dynamics in hunter-gatherer anthropology, and Tomasello's shared-intentionality comparative-cognition research.
independent_literatures: Fehr & Gächter experimental economics of cooperation
Tomasello comparative cognition and shared intentionality

convergences.name: Reproductive Motivation as Distinct Architecture
convergences.statement: Reproductive motivation (desire, attraction, pair-bonding) is a distinct architectural system independent of general-purpose pursuit, with sex-differentiated substrates and a characteristic proxy gradient from real partner to pure proxy - established independently by Panksepp's LUST-circuit affective neuroscience, Buss's sexual strategies theory and sex-differentiated mate preferences research, and Haselton/Buss's error-management prediction of sex-differentiated perceptual biases around mating cues.
independent_literatures: Haselton & Buss error management in cross-sex mind reading

convergences.name: Domain-Sensitive Organism Architecture
convergences.statement: The human organism contains evolved, domain-sensitive, interacting functional adaptations rather than a general-purpose learner - supported independently by Tooby & Cosmides' design-principle derivation, Panksepp's conserved subcortical affective-motivational systems, and Bowlby's attachment-as-primary-motivational-system framework.
independent_literatures: Tooby & Cosmides evolutionary psychology design principle

convergences.name: Systematic EEA-Modern Environment Mismatch
convergences.statement: Modern post-agricultural, post-industrial environments push evolved adaptations outside their expected operating ranges in systematic and predictable ways - established independently by Eaton & Konner's discordance hypothesis, Li/van Vugt/Colarelli's mismatch-identification framework, Boyd & Richerson's gene-culture coevolution constraint (matched must include cultural scaffolding), and Henrich's WEIRD empirical diagnostic showing Western populations anchor the extreme end of the cross-cultural distribution.
independent_literatures: Eaton & Konner evolutionary medicine / discordance hypothesis
Li van Vugt Colarelli mismatch hypothesis review

convergences.name: Phylogenetic Conservation of Subcortical Affective Systems
convergences.statement: The core affective-motivational systems (SEEKING, FEAR, RAGE, CARE, PANIC/GRIEF, PLAY, LUST) are anatomically and functionally conserved across mammals and extend into birds for specific systems - established independently by Panksepp's deep-brain-stimulation and cross-species neuroscience, Bowlby's attachment cross-mammalian homology, and Hrdy's cross-primate parental/alloparental evidence.

convergences.name: Error Management Asymmetry in Defensive Systems
convergences.statement: Defensive systems evolved under asymmetric error costs err reliably toward over-activation (false-positive) because the cost of missing a true threat historically exceeded the cost of reacting to a non-threat - established independently by Nesse's smoke-detector principle in evolutionary psychiatry, Haselton & Buss's Error Management Theory in evolutionary social psychology, and the Öhman/Mineka fear-module visual-attention program in cognitive neuroscience.
independent_literatures: Nesse smoke detector principle evolutionary psychiatry
Öhman & Mineka fear module cognitive neuroscience

convergences.name: Inclusive Fitness as Loss Function
convergences.statement: Natural selection operates on inclusive fitness - survival plus reproduction weighted by relatedness - establishing a single loss function that all evolved motivational architecture serves, as demonstrated independently by Darwinian selection theory, Hamilton's kin-selection formalism, and experimental altruistic-punishment findings that humans enforce cooperation at personal cost where inclusive-fitness logic predicts.
independent_literatures: Fehr & Gächter experimental economics of altruistic punishment

convergences.name: Allostatic Load Accumulation
convergences.statement: Chronic unresolved activation of stress-response systems produces cumulative physiological damage across multiple organ systems (allostatic load), reversible in part by environmental correction - established independently by McEwen's neuroendocrinology of allostasis and allostatic load and Sapolsky's primate stress physiology linking hierarchy type to cortisol and downstream pathology. The ACE Study was a third leg until 21 Nov 2026 and is withdrawn: it is a link from adults' own recall. The convergence now stands on two lines.
independent_literatures: McEwen allostasis and allostatic load neuroendocrinology

convergences.name: Adverse Experience Cascading Dose-Response
convergences.statement: Chronic adverse load cascades across physiological systems, with effects that propagate and self-maintain across domains (metabolic, immune, neural, behavioral) - established independently by McEwen's allostatic-load neuroendocrinology and Panksepp's cross-system inhibition evidence for affective-system propagation. The ACE Study was a third leg, and the source of the dose-response wording in the name, until 21 Nov 2026 and is withdrawn: it is a link from adults' own recall, about half of it is carried by genes and family for psychiatric outcomes, and a genetic analysis found no significant effect (ext 1653) of childhood maltreatment on heart disease, diabetes or inflammation. The convergence now stands on two lines.

convergences.name: Heritable Individual Variation in Behavioral Traits
convergences.statement: Individual differences in human behavioral and psychological traits are substantially heritable in every adequately measured domain, established independently by twin designs (Polderman et al. 2015 meta-analysis of fifty years of twin studies: 17,804 traits from 2,748 publications, average reported heritability 49%), adoption and family designs (the Plomin program: significant genetic influence on all psychological traits with corroborating adoption evidence), and molecular SNP-heritability estimated from unrelated individuals (the Yang et al. 2010 GCTA line), with Turkheimer's three laws of behavior genetics as the canonical framing. Heritability is a population statistic under a given environment distribution, not individual determinism.
independent_literatures: Plomin adoption and family designs (behavior genetics)

convergences.name: Aversive Outputs as Intelligible Defensive Signals
convergences.statement: Where no clear physical defect is the cause, aversive psychological and physiological outputs (anxiety, low mood, pain, grief, fatigue, anger) are intelligible defensive signals produced by architecture that is functioning correctly in response to inputs outside its expected operating range - established independently by Nesse's 'good reasons for bad feelings' evolutionary psychiatry, Panksepp's affective neuroscience of conserved aversive systems, and Fehr & Gächter's finding that anger/moralistic outrage is the proximate mechanism for prosocial norm enforcement rather than a dysregulation.
independent_literatures: Nesse evolutionary psychiatry of defensive signals
Panksepp affective neuroscience of aversive systems
Fehr & Gächter experimental economics of moralistic outrage

convergences.name: Developmental Calibration within Evolved Ranges
convergences.statement: Specific physiological and behavioral systems calibrate during specific developmental windows to environmental inputs within evolved parameters; inputs far outside those parameters leave a lasting mark - established independently by the Bucharest randomised trial of foster care against institutional rearing, the English and Romanian Adoptees natural experiment, and cross-fostering experiments in rats, with McEwen's HPA-axis neuroendocrinology as the bodily route. Inside the ordinary range of homes, differences in upbringing explain little of how adults differ in personality and attachment: adoptive siblings reared together correlate .04 in personality (ext 2880), and attachment in infancy showed no significant link with attachment more than 15 years later (ext 2893). Recalled childhood adversity (the ACE Study) was a leg of this convergence until 21 Nov 2026 and is withdrawn: it is a link from adults' own recall.
independent_literatures: Nelson, Zeanah and Fox Bucharest Early Intervention Project (randomised trial)
Rutter and Sonuga-Barke English and Romanian Adoptees study (natural experiment)
Meaney and Francis cross-fostering in rats (experimental neuroendocrinology)

mechanisms.name: Threat Management
mechanisms.description: Defensive system responding to threat cues. Includes offensive mode (frustration-aggression) absorbed from old M3 RAGE.
mechanisms.eli5: Detects danger. Makes you freeze, fight, or flee.
mechanisms.resolution_conditions: Safety established, threat eliminated or avoided.
mechanisms.mismatch_prediction: Modern threats - debt, emails, social media, status anxiety - can't be fought or fled. System stays on.
mechanisms.phylogenetic_age: ~460-535Myr (defence centre, all vertebrates); amygdala circuit ~340Myr+ (four-limbed vertebrates)

proxy_gradient.preamble: 5 levels (resolvability/actionability axis; true DA4 proxy only at floor)

mechanisms.name: Pursuit / Exploration
mechanisms.description: General-purpose seeking system. Sexual motivation belongs to M14. M2 resolves through real-world challenges that produce tangible outcomes: goal progress, skill building, resource acquisition.
mechanisms.eli5: Drives you to explore, pursue goals, and engage with the world.
mechanisms.resolution_conditions: Engagement with real challenges producing tangible outcomes.
mechanisms.mismatch_prediction: Variable-reward apps fire SEEKING without resolution. Open loop.
mechanisms.phylogenetic_age: ~460-535Myr (dopamine basal ganglia, all vertebrates; contested); reward pathway ~165Myr+ (mammals)

proxy_gradient.raw: 5 levels (cue constant = SEEKING/wanting; ordered by tangible outcome + consummatory-liking closure supplied, not by cue strength): engaging a real challenge that yields a real outcome (FULL; EVIDENCED) → knowledge work with a real but abstracted, delayed outcome (PARTIAL) → variable-reward app/feed with intermittent real payoff (MIXED) → infinite novelty, content scroll/idle browsing (MINIMAL) → machine gambling engineered for time-on-device with guaranteed net loss (ZERO; EVIDENCED). The order of MIXED (app) and MINIMAL (scroll) is untested.
proxy_gradient.preamble: 5 levels (cue constant = SEEKING/wanting; ordered by tangible outcome + consummatory-liking closure supplied, not by cue strength)
proxy_gradient.trailing: The order of MIXED (app) and MINIMAL (scroll) is untested.

mechanisms.name: Social Bonding
mechanisms.description: Attachment and co-regulation system. Includes grief mode (absorbed from old M9 GRIEF). Two states: security (enables broadly) and grief (suppresses broadly).
mechanisms.eli5: Forms bonds with other humans. Pain-grade distress when they're gone.
mechanisms.resolution_conditions: Reliable human co-regulation through physical presence, operating through nested social layers: ~5 intimate co-regulators (primary emotional/physical support), ~15 sympathy group, ~50 close social partners, ~150 coherent face-to-face relationships (Dunbar number - outer cognitive ceiling). Each layer represents qualitatively different relationship types with different obligations and investment requirements. The innermost ~5 provide the majority of social regulation; the critical variable at this layer is reliability, not count. The ~150 outer figure is an illustrative central tendency, not a hard limit: its derivation from the primate neocortex-ratio regression is contested (Lindenfors, Wartel & Lind 2021). What the evidence carries is the nested layering and the reliability-over-count point, not the exact rung figures; the layered structure and its low-hundreds clustering are separately observed in phone, Christmas-card, and Facebook data.
mechanisms.mismatch_prediction: Nuclear family, isolated living, mediated contact substituting for physical presence.
mechanisms.phylogenetic_age: ~165-200Myr (attachment, mammals); human layered network not dated

proxy_gradient.raw: 5 levels (ordered by real co-regulatory function supplied, not amount of contact): reliable physically co-present inner circle (FULL) → real bonded inner circle held at a distance, remote contact (PARTIAL) → large mediated network routing only partly to real co-presence (MIXED) → one-sided parasocial attachment to a non-reciprocating figure (MINIMAL) → AI companion engineered to simulate a reciprocating bond (ZERO; EVIDENCED-theoretical on ext595). Off-gradient: isolated/solo living = empty-shelf deprivation, not a rung.
proxy_gradient.preamble: 5 levels (ordered by real co-regulatory function supplied, not amount of contact)
proxy_gradient.trailing: Off-gradient: isolated/solo living = empty-shelf deprivation, not a rung.

real bonded inner circle held at a distance, remote contact

mechanisms.name: Social Calibration / Play
mechanisms.description: Play system develops social skills. Absent in threatened or ill animals.
mechanisms.eli5: Learns social rules through rough-and-tumble play. Requires real playmates.
mechanisms.resolution_conditions: Self-directed, unsupervised physical play with other children. In forager childhoods this is a mixed-age group.
mechanisms.mismatch_prediction: Structured activities replacing free play. Screens replacing bodies. Play deprivation.
mechanisms.phylogenetic_age: ~60Myr+ (social play, all primates; up to ~170Myr if one mammal system); play in reptiles and fish arose separately

proxy_gradient.raw: 5 levels (cue ≈ constant PLAY/SEEKING social-joy pull, fired in attenuated/substitute form at lower screen levels; ordered by how much real embodied reciprocity with an identity-bearing partner survives): self-directed, unsupervised physical play with other children, mixed-age as in forager childhoods (FULL; EVIDENCED) → adult-structured supervised physical activity, organized sports (PARTIAL) → screen-mediated multiplayer play with real peers (MIXED) → solitary single-player screen play, no reciprocating partner (MINIMAL) → engineered companion-AI / supernormal variable-reward 'play' product (ZERO; architecture-derived). The order of MIXED (screen play with real peers) and MINIMAL (solitary game) is untested.

mechanisms.name: Status Monitoring
mechanisms.description: Rank regulation. Shame, pride, submission, defeat, rank vigilance. Not optional - runs continuously.
mechanisms.eli5: Constantly monitors where you stand relative to others.
mechanisms.resolution_conditions: Acceptable position in a bounded, personally-known reference group on the order of ~150 (an illustrative central tendency, not a hard number; the precise figure is contested per Lindenfors 2021). Earned prestige preferred over coerced dominance. Prestige and dominance are separate routes to rank (Henrich & Gil-White 2001, work 129; Cheng et al. 2013, ext 622). Among the Chabu, prestige predicted elected leadership more strongly than dominance (Garfield & Hagen 2020, ext 624). Among Tsimane men, both routes went with higher fertility, and prestige was the strongest path from status to fitness (von Rueden et al. 2011, ext 623).
mechanisms.mismatch_prediction: Global comparison via social media. Millions of "peers." Status-defeat cascade.
mechanisms.phylogenetic_age: ~420-445Myr (rank circuit, bony vertebrates); rank-linked health ~25-34Myr+ (Old World primates)

The order of the two floor rungs (MINIMAL social-media comparison, ZERO purchased signals) is untested.

mechanisms.name: Circadian Regulation
mechanisms.description: SCN master clock. Gates metabolism, immunity, cognition, mood. The mismatch lies in timing more than in sleep duration. A week of natural light moved the body clock about two hours earlier while sleep duration stayed the same (Wright et al. 2013, ext 610, n=8). Social jetlag predicts overweight after controlling for sleep duration (Roenneberg et al. 2012, ext 92). Across 43 studies of 231,648 people, social jetlag went with higher body mass index and 1.2 times the odds of overweight (Arab et al. 2024).
mechanisms.eli5: Synchronizes every system to the light-dark cycle. Master timing architecture.
mechanisms.resolution_conditions: Dark-cued sleep onset, bright daylight exposure, consistent rhythm.
mechanisms.mismatch_prediction: Electric light, blue screens, shift work, caffeine
mechanisms.phylogenetic_age: ~500Myr+ (animal clock genes, insects and vertebrates); cyanobacterial clocks are older but a separate origin

mechanisms.name: Care / Alloparenting
mechanisms.description: Parental and alloparental care system. Oxytocin/prolactin circuits.
mechanisms.eli5: Distributed care - the organism expects a village, not solo parenting.
mechanisms.resolution_conditions: A distributed care network rather than solo or dyadic parenting. mechanisms.mismatch_prediction: Nuclear family without alloparental network. Parent burnout cascade.

mechanisms.name: Movement / Regulatory
mechanisms.description: Physical activity as zeitgeber, anti-inflammatory, mood regulator.
mechanisms.eli5: Movement isn't just exercise - it activates repair mechanisms throughout the organism.
mechanisms.resolution_conditions: Movement that's part of daily life rather than set aside as 'exercise'. Hadza men walk about 11 to 13 km a day and women about 6 to 8 km, and the women also dig for several hours, all as a side effect of foraging (Pontzer et al. 2012 and Wood et al. 2021, GPS; ext 196, ext 3418; Hadza only).
mechanisms.mismatch_prediction: Sedentarism. Gym sessions as partial compensation.
mechanisms.phylogenetic_age: ~2Myr (human form, argued); older regulatory roles not dated

mechanisms.name: Cooperation / Alliance
mechanisms.description: Reciprocity + norm enforcement + alliance dynamics. Convergence C11 forces M11. Four literatures support it (Fehr & Gächter, Boehm, Tomasello, Trivers). Its grade is strongly supported, one step below the top tier.
mechanisms.eli5: Reciprocal exchange, cheater detection, coalitional identity.
mechanisms.resolution_conditions: Trusted reciprocal network with norm enforcement within a group small enough for direct reputation tracking (on the order of ~150 - the same low-hundreds ceiling that bounds M3; the precise figure is contested per Lindenfors 2021). Norm enforcement requires repeated direct interaction where defectors can be identified, remembered, and sanctioned. Beyond that ceiling, cooperation requires institutional scaffolding (formal rules, third-party enforcement, shared fictions) rather than direct reciprocity. No shared fiction at the direct-reciprocity layer.
mechanisms.mismatch_prediction: Anonymous transactions, ghosting, no shared narrative.
mechanisms.phylogenetic_age: ~25-34Myr+ (reciprocity, Old World primates); human norm enforcement under ~10Myr

forced_by_convergence.name: Reproductive Motivation as Distinct Architecture
forced_by_convergence.statement: Reproductive motivation (desire, attraction, pair-bonding) is a distinct architectural system independent of general-purpose pursuit, with sex-differentiated substrates and a characteristic proxy gradient from real partner to pure proxy - established independently by Panksepp's LUST-circuit affective neuroscience, Buss's sexual strategies theory and sex-differentiated mate preferences research, and Haselton/Buss's error-management prediction of sex-differentiated perceptual biases around mating cues.

forced_by_convergence.name: Phylogenetic Conservation of Subcortical Affective Systems
forced_by_convergence.statement: The core affective-motivational systems (SEEKING, FEAR, RAGE, CARE, PANIC/GRIEF, PLAY, LUST) are anatomically and functionally conserved across mammals and extend into birds for specific systems - established independently by Panksepp's deep-brain-stimulation and cross-species neuroscience, Bowlby's attachment cross-mammalian homology, and Hrdy's cross-primate parental/alloparental evidence.

forced_by_convergence.name: Socially Scaffolded Regulation via Attachment
forced_by_convergence.statement: Human regulation is constitutively socially scaffolded: the organism's default expectation is proximity to trusted co-regulators, and this scaffolding is architectural rather than optional - established independently by Coan's Social Baseline Theory fMRI program, Bowlby's attachment theory, Hrdy's cooperative-breeding thesis, Dunbar's social-brain hypothesis, and Holt-Lunstad's mortality meta-analysis showing 50% survival advantage from strong social relationships.

parameters.name: Social network layers (~5/15/50/150)
parameters.eea_baseline: The ancestral social world was structured as a series of hierarchically inclusive, nested relationship layers, each roughly three times the size of the one inside it: an innermost support clique of ~5 close confidants who provided emotional and physical support, a sympathy group of ~15 (people whose loss would be deeply felt, contacted at least monthly), an affinity/band layer of ~50 (the typical overnight foraging camp of casual-but-close associates), and an active personal network of ~150 (the clan/tribal layer, the outer ceiling of stable, individually-known relationships). Each layer carried a qualitatively different grade of intimacy, obligation, and contact frequency, with the heaviest investment concentrated in the inner ~5-15. The ~150 outer figure is an illustrative central tendency, not a constant: traditional tribal and clan groupings cluster in the low hundreds. Its original derivation from the primate neocortex-ratio regression fails re-analysis (Lindenfors, Wartel and Lind 2021), so the specific number is treated as approximate; what is load-bearing is the nested layering, not the precise ceiling. This was the full architecture within which status was monitored and alliances tracked: a personally-known reference group bounded at ~150, not an anonymous mass.

eea_value.outer_ceiling_note: low hundreds; ~150 is an approximate central tendency, not a constant; the neocortex-ratio derivation is contested (Lindenfors 2021)

parameters.modern_default: The modern environment delivers a radically inverted network shape: nominal friend/follower counts in the hundreds or thousands that vastly exceed the ~150 cognitive ceiling, while the layers that actually carry support and intimacy stay capacity-bounded. Online networks reproduce the same ~5/15 inner structure when genuine ties are measured (support clique ~4, sympathy group ~14, statistically indistinguishable from offline values), and mean platform friend counts hover near ~150-190 (across all 721 million Facebook users of May 2011 the mean was about 190 and the median 99; Ugander et al. 2011, ext 4624), but the bulk of nominal connections are inactive labels rather than relationships (only ~27.6% of online 'friends' are reported as genuine). Inner-layer bonds decay back toward mere acquaintance without the face-to-face contact the architecture was built to expect; mediated contact slows but does not substitute for it. The result is a wide, shallow periphery of weak or fictive ties layered on top of a core that the larger network does not, and cannot, enlarge: among 117 adults, more time on social media went with more online friends and with no larger or emotionally closer offline network (Pollet, Roberts and Dunbar 2011).
parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is not in the inner-layer capacities themselves (still ~5/15/50/150, not technologically expandable) but between the number of ties the modern environment presents (hundreds to thousands of nominal contacts) and the number the brain can actually monitor and invest in (~150, with real support concentrated in the inner ~5-15). People with unusually large networks do not gain more close friends; they accumulate weakly-defined acquaintances. Status monitoring (M5) and alliance/reputation tracking (M11), evolved for a ~150 personally-known reference group, are now flooded by reference groups orders of magnitude larger and largely composed of strangers, while the trust-bearing inner layers remain capped and are under-fed when face-to-face contact is displaced.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (22 Nov 2026): tested many times for the layering. Forager populations were organised in nested levels, each about three to four times the size of the one below, across 339 societies in Binford's compilation (Hamilton et al. 2007, ext 1048: families of about 4.5, dispersed groups of 15.6, residential groups of 54, periodic gatherings of 165). Personal networks fall into nested layers about three times the size of the one inside in pooled published group sizes (Zhou et al. 2005, ext 2042), phone records of 34.9 million users (Mac Carron, Kaski and Dunbar 2016, ext 2026), and Facebook and Twitter contact data (Dunbar et al. 2015, ext 4336; Arnaboldi et al. 2016, ext 3323). A model with one fixed capacity for relationships, in which closer ties cost more, reproduces the layers, and about 98 percent of 84 students' networks showed them with a scaling ratio of about 2.7 to 3.1 (Tamarit et al. 2018). Main weakness: the forager levels are group sizes, not one person's network, and the modern network data all come from Dunbar's group and its collaborators. The 150 figure fails re-analysis of the primate regression it came from (Lindenfors, Wartel and Lind 2021, ext 619), so the layer sizes and the 150 ceiling are approximate. Forager residential groups are fluid (Bird et al. 2019, ext 684), which concerns who shares a camp, not the layers of a person's network.

parameters.name: Lifetime known-individual ceiling (~1,000)
parameters.eea_baseline: Across a foraging lifetime an individual accumulated a bounded pool of personally known others - people met face-to-face, named, placed in a kin/alliance/reputation map, and remembered. Estimates put this cumulative lifetime roster at roughly 1,000+ distinct individuals (Hill et al. 2014, Hadza/Ache), an order of magnitude above the ~150 actively-maintained network the social brain tracks concurrently. This pool was not a single contemporaneous group: it accreted over decades through camp reshuffling, regional fission-fusion, and durable cross-camp partnerships (e.g. Ju/'hoansi hxaro). Crucially it was finite, slowly-growing, and fully reputation-indexed: nearly everyone one would ever encounter was either already known or one or two reciprocal links away, and almost no one was a true anonymous stranger. The cognitive machinery for naming, tracking reputation, and gauging trust was calibrated to a lifetime ceiling on this order, with the ~150 active-network limit (Dunbar) operating as the concurrent sub-ceiling within it.

eea_value.note: Hill et al. 2014 (Ache, Hadza; ext 606, 608): a 'social universe of about a thousand individuals'; a lifetime pool 'clearly more than 1,000'. One model-based study in two populations. For the ~150 ceiling and the 5/15/50/150 layers, see EEA-SOC-01.

parameters.modern_default: A networked individual is exposed to vastly more than 1,000 distinct identities - thousands of nominal "friends"/followers plus a near-unbounded daily stream of strangers (crowds, feeds, comment sections, customer interactions). Nominal contact counts routinely run into the thousands while the genuinely-tracked inner network stays pinned near the same ~150, and only ~27.6% of those nominal ties register as genuine close friends. The result is a permanent flood of identities the reputation-tracking and trust-calibration system was never built to index: most are anonymous, non-reciprocal, never re-encountered, and carry no durable reputation, so they neither enter the lifetime roster nor decay out of it normally - they simply accumulate as un-indexable noise. The pool of actually-known, reputation-bearing people is no larger than ancestrally, but it is now embedded in an environment of effectively infinite strangers.
parameters.gap_statement: EEA delivered a finite, slowly-accreting lifetime roster (~1,000+) in which virtually every encountered person was known or one reciprocal link away and carried trackable reputation; modernity delivers an unbounded firehose of identities, the overwhelming majority anonymous, non-reciprocal, and reputation-less. The mismatch is not in the size of the maintainable network (still ~150) but in the ratio of known-to-unknown: a system tuned to "almost everyone you meet is someone you can place" now operates where almost everyone you meet is someone you cannot. This chronically engages strangers as ambient novelty/threat (threat-management framing) and starves the cooperation/reputation system (M11) of the direct, repeated, reciprocal observability it evolved to run on, while the cumulative roster of genuinely-known people fails to grow despite massive nominal connection.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested once. One study estimates a lifetime pool of over 1,000 people from interaction rates and life tables in Ache and Hadza (Hill et al. 2014); model-based, two populations.

parameters.name: Band / camp size (a few dozen adults; ~25-50)
parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral humans lived in small, residentially co-present foraging bands (camps): a single overnight camp typically held on the order of a few dozen adults - roughly 25 to 50, with central estimates clustering near ~28-35 - a scale that sits within the Dunbar 'band' layer (~35) and 'overnight camp' layer (~50) of the nested social network. At this scale every co-resident is a personally known, named individual whose behaviour can be directly observed and tracked over time. Band size was thus bounded well below the ~150 active-network ceiling, keeping the day-to-day social field small enough that cooperation, status, and bonding all operated face-to-face among mutually familiar people rather than among anonymous strangers.

eea_value.units: co-resident adults in a single band / overnight camp
eea_value.source_status: Band about 35 (Dunbar 1998, ext 490) and overnight camp about 50 (Dunbar 2010, ext 404). Median residential group of 27 people across 263 forager societies (Marlowe 2005, ext 754). The mean of 28.2 adults across 32 societies is attributed to Hill et al. 2011 (work 172); Cor's extraction from that work (ext 683) covers relatedness and does not carry the figure.

parameters.modern_default: Modern humans do not live in a single bounded, personally-known residential band. Daily life is partitioned across many large, partly anonymous groupings - workplaces, apartment buildings, transit systems, schools, and online networks - most of which exceed the ~25-50 face-to-face band scale and many of which exceed the ~150 ceiling entirely. A person routinely shares physical or digital space with hundreds or thousands of unfamiliar individuals while their actual co-regulating relationships shrink. The small, stable, fully-known co-resident group of a few dozen adults has no direct modern equivalent; its functions are split across institutions where most co-present others are strangers.
parameters.gap_statement: The ancestral social field was a small set of a few dozen (~25-50) personally-known adults sharing a camp, sitting within the band/overnight-camp Dunbar layer. The modern default replaces this with chronic immersion in groupings far larger than the band scale, dominated by unfamiliar people, while genuinely co-regulating relationships number far fewer than the band once held. The delta is a mismatch between the scale at which our cooperation, status-monitoring, and bonding machinery was calibrated (a bounded, fully-known band/camp of a few dozen adults) and the scale we actually inhabit (large, partly anonymous aggregations plus a thin set of disposable ties), so the band-sized layer that once carried daily social life is no longer delivered by any single modern structure.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Residential group size is measured across many forager societies: Marlowe 2005 (263 societies, median 27 people of all ages) and Hill et al. 2011 (32 societies, mean 28.2 adults). The range is wide (13 to 250 people across Marlowe's 263 societies, ext 754); Singh and Glowacki 2022 (ext 756) argue that larger, settled non-agricultural groups also existed in the Late Pleistocene.

parameters.name: Within-camp kin fraction (low; campmates mostly unrelated)
parameters.eea_baseline: A person's residential camp/band was NOT a clan of close relatives. Across forager societies the typical residential group (~25-50 people, ~28 adults) was composed mostly of individuals to whom the focal person was not closely related: primary/first-order kin (parents, siblings, offspring) made up only a small minority of co-residents (under 10% of a residential camp; Apicella et al. 2012, ext 601), and most campmates were unrelated or only distantly related. Because residence was bilocal/sex-egalitarian (couples lived with both the husband's and the wife's kin over time) and camps reshuffled frequently, genetic relatedness within a camp was low. The practical consequence: the durable social glue holding a camp together was NOT shared genes. The bonds that mattered, and that were conserved across the constant churn, were reciprocal, trust-based, reputation-tracked relationships between individuals who chose each other, not kin ties imposed by birth.

eea_value.source_caveat: Low within-camp relatedness: Hill et al. 2011 (PMID 21393537, 32-society co-residence census) is in Cor as work 172, background tier (ext 683); Dyble et al. 2015 (PMID 25977551) is in Cor as work 176, background tier (ext 687). The under-10 percent primary-kin figure is verbatim in Apicella et al. 2012 (work 115, core, ext 601) and Smith et al. 2018 gives primary kin per camp (work 116, core, ext 605); both are Hadza, so the figure is Hadza-anchored. Camp size range is illustrative.
eea_value.relatedness_qualitative: low; most campmates unrelated or distantly related

parameters.modern_default: Modern social environments invert the ancestral pattern in two opposite directions at once. (1) The family one is biologically related to is now small, seldom all within reach (in the US three in four adults have a parent or grown child within 30 miles, about a third have all of them that near, and 13 percent share a home with one; Choi et al. 2020, ext 4204), and often the ONLY kin one regularly co-resides with, so the kin one has are concentrated in a tiny stable household rather than diffused through a larger chosen group. (2) The larger groups one spends daily life inside (workplace, neighborhood, online networks, institutions) are composed of effectively unrelated strangers, but unlike the ancestral camp these groupings are NOT self-assembled through mutual choice, reciprocity, and reputation tracking; membership is assigned by employment, address, or platform. The result is that 'who you live and work among' is no longer the output of a relationship-selection process; it is administratively or commercially determined, and the unrelated people around you are frequently strangers you did not choose and do not reciprocally track.
parameters.gap_statement: The ancestral signal was: 'the group around me is mostly unrelated people I (or my band) actively chose and continuously vetted through reciprocity and reputation; kinship is not what holds us together, the relationships are.' The modern signal is degraded on the selection axis: the unrelated people around us are still mostly unrelated (that part matches), but they are assigned rather than chosen, and the reciprocity/reputation machinery that turned unrelated campmates into durable trusted allies is largely absent or shallow. Mechanisms M3 (bonding) and M11 (cooperation/alliance) evolved expecting that low kin-relatedness would be compensated by self-selected, reciprocal, reputation-anchored dyads. Modernity delivers the low relatedness WITHOUT the compensating chosen-and-vetted dyadic structure, so the mechanisms fire in a world of unrelated-but-also-unbonded co-residents, which is a key part of why being surrounded by people can still register as social isolation.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Low relatedness within camps comes from a 32-society co-residence census (Hill et al. 2011) and is repeated by separate teams in Hadza, Agta and BaYaka (Apicella et al. 2012; Dyble et al. 2015); the under-10-percent primary-kin figure is Hadza-anchored.

evidence.author_quote: We present an agent-based model suggesting that, even if all individuals in a community seek to live with as many kin as possible, within-camp relatedness is reduced if men and women have equal influence in selecting camp members. parameters.name: Membership turnover (camp dissolves and reconstitutes; most campmates change between survey waves)
parameters.eea_baseline: The residential group (camp/band) was a fission-fusion structure that continuously dissolved and reconstituted rather than a fixed-membership unit. Among the best-studied foragers (Hadza), entire camps relocated roughly every 4-8 weeks and individuals reshuffled across camps such that only a minority of campmates carried over from one survey wave to the next (Smith et al. 2018, Hadza waves 1 to 3 years apart; the exact proportion is unverified, see eea_value). Crucially, despite this high residential churn, assortment on cooperation persisted (cooperators clustered together across reshuffles), and what was conserved across the turnover was not the group but the durable, individually-tracked reciprocal relationships between specific people. Group composition was fluid; the dyadic ties were the stable substrate.

eea_value.source: Smith et al. 2018, Current Biology, doi 10.1016/j.cub.2018.07.064 (Hadza; survey waves 2010, 2013, 2014, 2016); in Cor as core work 116
eea_value.repeated_campmates_status: UNVERIFIED: the published Current Biology text has not been read. The two preprint versions disagree because they define the measure differently: bioRxiv 313064v1 reports 12.1% (people lived with at both waves divided by all unique people lived with at either wave); v2 reports 21.9% (share of campmates at one wave still living with the person at the next). Waves are 1 to 3 years apart, so neither is an annual rate.

parameters.modern_default: Modern social environments invert the structure: the GROUP labels are stable and durable (a workplace, a school cohort, a neighborhood, a social-media platform or feed) while the actual dyadic relationships within them are shallow, interchangeable, and disposable. People remain nominal members of named, persistent groups for years, yet cycle through co-members with little individual reciprocal investment, and there is no institution analogous to a delayed-reciprocity partnership (e.g. hxaro) that conserves a specific bond once physical proximity ends. Relationships routinely lapse the moment shared context (job, class, proximity) is removed.
parameters.gap_statement: The ancestral and modern environments are inverted on which layer is stable. Ancestrally the GROUP churned (most campmates changed between survey waves) while the durable reciprocal DYAD was conserved across the churn; the relationship, not the group, was the unit that persisted. Modernity delivers the opposite: stable, durable group labels (workplace, cohort, feed) paired with shallow, disposable dyads and no mechanism (no hxaro-equivalent) for conserving a specific bond once proximity ends. The mismatch lies in where turnover lands: on the relationships, which evolved to persist, instead of on group membership, which evolved to be fluid. That leaves the co-regulating, reputation-tracking reciprocal dyad chronically unmet.
parameters.resolution_unit: The durable reciprocal dyad - a specific, individually-known partner with whom reciprocity, co-regulation, and reputation are tracked over years. What needs conserving across membership turnover is not the group or the amount of contact but the persistence of particular bonded relationships; the bond, not the band, is the conserved unit.
parameters.confidence_note: Smith et al. 2018 (Hadza; ext 602). The preprint figures (12.1% in v1, 21.9% in v2) use different definitions, and the published figure has not been read. Survey waves are 1 to 3 years apart, so neither figure is an annual rate. Single Hadza population.

evidence.author_quote: Across the three intervals, the mean proportion of repeated campmates was 12.1%.
evidence.content: Across 6 years / 4 waves, Hadza camps continuously dissolve and reconstitute: only about 12% of campmates repeat from one survey wave to the next (waves 1 to 3 years apart), yet cooperative assortment persists.

evidence.author_quote: Every 4-8 weeks entire camps shift location usually in response to resource availability.
evidence.content: Camp membership is fission-fusion: entire camps relocate on a weeks timescale, so the group as a unit does not persist.

parameters.name: Selection rule / "shuffle algorithm" (choice-driven; homophily + cooperation + reciprocity; kinship not main glue)
parameters.eea_baseline: Who you lived alongside was not assigned by birth or fixed institution but produced by an ongoing, choice-driven assortment process operating across frequent residential reshuffling. In Hadza camps this "algorithm" had recurring structure: (1) homophily - co-residence was more likely between people similar in age, height, weight, body fat, and handgrip strength; (2) strong reciprocity - naming was near-symmetric, with an ego roughly 37-51x (point ~44x) more likely to name an alter who named them; (3) cooperator assortment - cooperators clustered with cooperators, an association extending out to two degrees of separation in gift networks; plus transitivity and geographic decay. Crucially, kinship was NOT the main glue: people actively sorted on disposition and reciprocity, not primarily on relatedness. The output was a camp continually re-composed of preferred, reciprocating, similarly-cooperative partners.
parameters.modern_default: Group membership is overwhelmingly assigned rather than self-assorted: workplaces, school classes, residential buildings, and algorithmically-curated feeds place you among people you did not choose and who did not choose you. Where modern matching exists (dating apps, professional networks, recommender feeds), the optimization target is engagement, novelty, or proximity-of-the-moment - not durable mutual reciprocity, demonstrated cooperativeness, or transitive trust within a personally-known group. The ancestral feedback loop (you preferentially co-reside with people who reciprocate your investment and who others vouch for, observed directly over time) is largely absent; assortment on cooperation is replaced by assortment on platform metrics or institutional convenience.
parameters.gap_statement: The EEA delivered a continuous, agency-rich sorting process that filtered one's immediate social world toward reciprocating, cooperative, vouched-for partners - kinship was secondary. The modern environment inverts this: membership in one's daily groups is mostly imposed (employer, building, algorithm), and the explicit matching systems that do exist optimize for engagement/novelty rather than reciprocity and demonstrated cooperation. The result is reduced control over WHO populates one's social field, weaker assortment on actual cooperativeness, and loss of the transitive-reputation signal that let ancestral humans cluster with trustworthy reciprocators out to two degrees. The mismatch is not "fewer people" but a broken selection rule: the inputs the ancestral algorithm ran on (mutual choice, observed reciprocity, cooperator reputation) are no longer the primary determinants of who one lives and works among.
parameters.confidence_note: Shuffle algorithm now grounded in Apicella 2012 full text: trait homophily, strong reciprocity (44.2x campmate / 14.3x gift), and social distance as important as genetic relatedness (kinship not the sole glue). Single Hadza population; kept thin.

evidence.author_quote: An "ego" (the naming person) is 44.2 times (95% C.I. 37.6 to 51.4) more likely to name an "alter" (the named person) in the campmate network, and 14.3 times (95% C.I. 12.2 to 16.4) more likely to name an alter in the gift network, if the alter reciprocated the social tie by also naming the ego as a friend
evidence.content: Hadza campmate/gift networks show strong dyadic reciprocity even though nominations are private and controlling for kin ties.

evidence.author_quote: in both the campmate and gift networks, social ties are significantly more likely when two people are similar in age, height, weight, body fat, and handgrip strength.
evidence.content: Homophily in Hadza social ties runs on age and physical/condition traits (the "shuffle" is similarity-driven, not random).

evidence.author_quote: social distance appears to be as important as genetic relatedness and physical proximity in explaining assortativity in cooperation
evidence.content: Cooperative assortment in Hadza networks: similarity in cooperation extends to two degrees, and social distance rivals genetic relatedness in explaining it (kinship is not the sole glue).

parameters.name: Relationship longevity & maintenance (decades-long durable dyads; ~27-yr co-survival ceiling; maintenance institutions like hxaro conserve bonds across distance)
parameters.eea_baseline: In ancestral foraging life the load-bearing social unit was the durable, reciprocal DYAD, not the group. Because groups continuously reshuffled (camps fissioned/fused on the order of every ~4-8 weeks, with most campmates changing from one survey wave to the next), what was conserved across the churn was the relationship itself, sustained for decades by both face-to-face co-presence when proximity allowed AND by explicit maintenance institutions when it did not. Among the Ju/'hoansi, hxaro was a formal delayed-reciprocity gift-partnership system reported to begin in childhood, be kept for life, be inherited at death, and span dispersed bands up to ~200 km apart, with only a minority of a person's partners co-resident in the current camp, so a bond could persist even when the two partners were rarely or never in the same camp. Two adults who reached adulthood together could expect on the order of ~27 years of overlapping co-survival, and reciprocal alliances ran over that whole horizon. Trivers's conditions for the evolution of reciprocal altruism describe exactly this regime: a long lifetime, low dispersal, and repeated interaction with the same small set of individuals, so that an investment in a specific partner reliably paid back over time.

eea_value._note: The 200 km hxaro range and about 15 partners per adult come from Wiessner & Huang 2022 (ext 752; Ju/'hoansi, 1974). The ~27-year co-survival figure, the ~18% co-resident figure, and childhood onset and inheritance are attributed to Wiessner 2002, which is not in Cor and has not been read. For turnover: no number is used; see campmate_turnover_status. Camps shift every ~4-8 weeks (Smith et al. 2018, core work 116).
eea_value.campmate_turnover_status: UNVERIFIED: see EEA-SOC-05. Smith et al. 2018 (Hadza; in Cor as core work 116) preprint v1 reports 12.1% repeated campmates and v2 reports 21.9%, under different definitions; survey waves are 1 to 3 years apart, so neither is an annual rate; the published figure was not read.

parameters.modern_default: The modern environment inverts the ancestral pattern: it supplies stable GROUP labels (a workplace, a school cohort, a social-media feed, a city) while the dyads inside them are shallow and disposable, and there is no institutional equivalent of hxaro that conserves a specific bond once physical proximity ends. When two people stop sharing a context, the relationship is simply allowed to decay; nothing structurally obligates either party to keep servicing it. Empirically, friendships require recurring face-to-face contact to avoid sliding down through the network layers and eventually dropping out of the personal network entirely, and online media at best slows that decay rather than preventing it. Trust and bond depth track time invested in a relationship, and the maintenance cost (mainly time) scales roughly linearly with the number of relationships, so modern people spread thin investment across large, low-trust networks and let most ties lapse rather than maintaining a small set of partners across decades.
parameters.gap_statement: The ancestral environment conserved the relationship across changing groups; the modern environment conserves the group label and lets the relationships churn. The specific missing piece is a maintenance institution: the EEA had hxaro-type structures (formalized, inheritable, distance-spanning, long-term delayed reciprocity) that actively preserved a named dyad even with little or no co-presence, whereas modernity has no hxaro-equivalent and instead relies on shared proximity/context as the only glue. When that proximity ends (job change, move, leaving school), the bond is not migrated to an institution that keeps it alive; it decays. The result is many stable-looking memberships sitting on top of disposable, shallow ties, with the durable decades-long reciprocal partnership that M3/M11 are calibrated to expect largely absent.
parameters.resolution_unit: The durable, spatially-dispersed reciprocal DYAD plus the maintenance institutions that conserve it across distance and time - i.e., a specific named partner whose bond is actively serviced (face-to-face when possible, and via hxaro-type delayed-reciprocity exchange when apart) so the relationship persists for decades and survives the reshuffling of any particular group. Conserved across the churn is the relationship, not the group; the resolution requires migrating a bond to an institution that keeps it alive once proximity ends, not merely accumulating more low-investment ties.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade: tested once. Hxaro range and partner count: Wiessner & Huang 2022 (ext 752), Ju/'hoansi only. Co-survival and co-resident figures: Wiessner 2002, not in Cor and unread. Camps move every 4 to 8 weeks (Smith et al. 2018, ext 604, Hadza), and no turnover number is used (see EEA-SOC-05). Modern side: Dunbar proposes that friendships decay without face-to-face meetings and that social media only slow the decay (Dunbar 2016, ext 509, 510; cross-sectional data). In the model of Sutcliffe et al. 2012, the time cost of keeping relationships grows in line with their number, and trust grows with time invested (ext 503, 505; theoretical). Reciprocity is favoured by a long lifetime, low dispersal and repeated interaction with the same few individuals (Trivers 1971, ext 479).

parameters.name: Novel-stranger frequency (rare, salient, often a threat)
parameters.eea_baseline: Social cognition operated over a bounded pool: a personally-known reference network capped near the ~150 Dunbar ceiling, nested in ~5/15/50/150 layers of decreasing intimacy, the outermost being the people one recognizes and interacts with across a year. Within that architecture almost every face encountered was already known, placed, and reputationally tracked. A genuinely novel stranger - an individual who could not be located anywhere in one's known network or in the known networks of one's allies - was therefore a comparatively rare event. Because the bounded pool had no slot for such a person, novelty itself was diagnostic: a never-before-seen individual could not be vouched for, had no shared reputational history, and could not be assumed to be bound by the local web of reciprocity and norm enforcement. Encounters with unplaceable strangers were thus both infrequent and highly salient, and the threat-management system (M1) treated unfamiliarity as a plausible danger cue to be resolved (placed, vouched-for, or avoided) rather than as a routine background condition. This is an inference from the bounded-pool architecture plus M1, not a directly measured ancestral rate.
parameters.modern_default: The contemporary environment delivers a near-continuous stream of novel, unplaceable faces: dense urban crowds, transit, commerce, and especially the feeds and follower graphs of online platforms expose a person to more unfamiliar individuals in a single day than an ancestral forager might meet in a lifetime. Unfamiliarity is the modal condition rather than the rare exception, so the diagnostic value of novelty collapses - a stranger is no longer informative about anything. Yet the same M1 machinery still treats unplaceable others as potential threats, now firing against a constant baseline it was never calibrated for, while the reputational and vouching scaffolding that once resolved a stranger encounter is largely absent.
parameters.gap_statement: The delta is one of base rate and resolvability. Ancestrally, novel strangers were rare, salient, and resolvable (place them in the known web, or treat unfamiliarity as an actionable threat signal); modernity inverts this to constant, non-diagnostic, unresolvable novelty. The threat-management system inherited from the rare-stranger regime cannot down-regulate to the new base rate: it either over-fires (chronic low-grade vigilance, stranger-directed wariness in crowds and online) or, where it habituates, leaves people transacting with a stream of others who carry none of the reputational accountability the system implicitly assumes. The conserved unit being eroded is not the count of strangers but the durable, reputationally-tracked dyad against which any new face used to be evaluated; once almost everyone is a stranger, the bounded-pool premise that made novelty meaningful no longer holds.
parameters.resolution_unit: The durable, reputationally-tracked reciprocal dyad: ancestrally every new face was evaluated against a finite web of known, vouched-for relationships, and it was that web of bonds - not the count of strangers per se - that gave novelty its diagnostic and protective meaning. The mismatch resolves only insofar as new encounters can be anchored back into durable, accountable relationships rather than left as anonymous one-off contacts.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade: argued, not yet tested. No study measures how often ancestral humans met strangers. The premise is a bounded pool of personally known people in nested layers of about 5, 12, 35 and 150 (Dunbar 1998, ext 490), with a limit on how many relationships a person can monitor at once (Dunbar 1992, ext 485). For the stranger-as-threat side: in chimpanzees, lethal raids by males from neighbouring groups are a major cause of death (Hrdy 2009, ext 383), and across 18 communities most killings were by males and of members of other communities (Wilson et al. 2014, ext 671). This is animal evidence. Ambush killing between groups is documented in several nomadic forager societies, and how often it happened is disputed (Wrangham & Glowacki 2012, ext 672; Bowles 2009, ext 673). Infants show wariness toward an approaching stranger in lab studies (Waters et al. 1975, ext 676). Against it: in 21 mobile forager bands most recorded killings were homicides, a few were feuds and a minority were war (Fry & Söderberg 2013, ext 674), and Tomasello describes cooperation with in-group strangers (Tomasello 2014, ext 238, 250). Bowlby's claim that strangers are an innate fear cue (ext 574) comes from a book that was not read directly and is not linked as evidence.

evidence.content: The number of neocortical neurons limits information-processing capacity, which constrains the number of relationships an individual can monitor simultaneously. The constraint operates on relationship structure and quality, not raw number of dyads.

evidence.content: In chimpanzees, attacks from conspecifics - including infanticide and lethal raids by bands of males from neighboring groups - are major sources of mortality.

evidence.content: Across 18 chimpanzee communities studied over five decades, killings (recorded in 15 of them) were mostly by males and mostly of members of other communities, and killing rates did not track measures of human disturbance.

Killing between groups of nomadic hunter-gatherers tends to fit the chimpanzee pattern of surprise attacks when one side greatly outnumbers the other. Humans also form peaceful ties and alliances between groups, which chimpanzees do not.

parameters.name: Behavioral observability / reputation visibility
parameters.eea_baseline: In a band/camp embedded in a personally-known reference group of roughly 150 individuals, virtually all of a person's relevant behavior was directly observable by, or rapidly transmitted through gossip to, people who knew them by name, knew their history, and would interact with them again for decades. Reputation was a shared, continuously-updated, distributed record: as Boehm puts it, "the band keeps a dossier on every individual, noting positive and negative points." Where campmates differed, they knew it: asked one by one in 12 Hadza camps, they agreed more on who hunts best (r 0.23) and a little more on who works hardest (r 0.08). They barely agreed on who shares the most food, who tells the fewest lies and who has the best heart (ext 2795). Project position (21 Nov 2026): anyone still in camp shared and was honest enough to be kept there, so on those points there was little left to rank, and such labels sort strangers more than campmates. The study's authors read the low agreement as moral behaviour that changes across time and situations to fit local circumstances (ext 2796). Observability had teeth: those who deviated (theft, deception, stinginess, free-riding) were subject to gossip, ridicule, ostracism, and ultimately exclusion, and everyone knew this monitoring was constant, so it functioned as a deterrent and people exercised self-control accordingly. Because foraging was obligately collaborative, individuals had to continuously evaluate partners and track how they themselves were being evaluated. The net result: visibility was near-total, embodied, hard to fake over time, attached to a single durable identity, and backed by real consequences enforced by people one could not escape.

eea_value.identity: single durable identity, behavior history attached for life
eea_value.observability: near-total within band/camp; rapid gossip diffusion across the ~150 layer
eea_value.accountability: high: gossip, ridicule, ostracism, exclusion; non-exitable repeat interaction
eea_value.reference_group_basis: personally-known, named, repeat-interaction reference group (Dunbar ceiling)

parameters.modern_default: Most behavior now occurs among strangers or weak ties who do not know one's history and will never interact with one again, while the visibility that does exist is mediated, curated, and quantitatively inflated. On social platforms only ~27.6% of nominal "friends" are considered genuine close ties (with a strong modal value between 0 and 10%), so networks are padded with weakly-accountable acquaintances rather than people tracking one's actual conduct. Mediated contact cannot substitute for the embodied, face-to-face observation the bonding/reputation system evolved for: without periodic in-person contact, ties decay through the network layers into mere acquaintance regardless of online activity. Visibility is now selectively self-presented (gameable), fragmented across multiple personas and contexts, frequently pseudonymous or low-stakes, and policed (if at all) by distant institutions or algorithms rather than by named peers with whom one shares a future. Reputation is either absent (anonymity), sortable away (exit/blocking, fresh accounts), or captured by platform metrics that reward performance over honesty.
parameters.gap_statement: The ancestral environment delivered near-total, embodied, hard-to-fake, single-identity behavioral observability inside a ~150-person reference group whose members knew one's history and held real, inescapable enforcement power. The modern environment delivers visibility that is mediated, curated, gameable, fragmented across exitable contexts, padded with non-accountable weak ties, and largely stripped of peer-enforced consequences. The reputation-tracking machinery (M11) and status-position monitoring (M5) evolved to run on dense, durable, accountable observation now operate on thin, performative, low-accountability signals, producing both reputational impunity for defection among strangers and chronic exposure of curated personas to vast unfamiliar audiences with no reciprocal knowledge of the person behind them.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade: argued, not yet tested. Forager bands track reputation through gossip, ridicule and ostracism (Boehm 1999, ext 373, 375), and partners evaluate each other (Tomasello 2014, ext 239). The threat of gossip made people more generous in experiments (Feinberg et al. 2012, ext 719), and in 15 small-scale communities shame tracked how much the community would devalue an act (Sznycer et al. 2018, ext 722). Modern side: respondents counted only 27.6% of their Facebook friends as genuine (Dunbar 2016, ext 508), and Dunbar proposes that ties decay without face-to-face meetings (ext 509; cross-sectional data). Two meta-analyses found no evidence that artificial watching-eye cues raise generosity (Northover et al. 2017, ext 829). No study compares ancestral and modern observability directly. The comparison is the framework's reading.

evidence.author_quote: In the hypothesis of Tomasello et al. (2012), obligate collaborative foraging became an evolutionarily stable strategy for early humans because of two interrelated processes: interdependence and social selection. The first and most basic point is that humans began a lifestyle in which individuals could not procure their daily sustenance alone but instead were interdependent with others in their foraging activities - which meant that individuals needed to develop the skills and motivations to forage collaboratively or else starve. There was thus direct and immediate selective pressure for skills and motivations for joint collaborative activity (joint intentionality). The second point is that as a natural outcome of this interdependence, individuals began to make evaluative judgments about others as potential collaborative partners: they began to be socially selective, since choosing a poor partner meant less food. Cheaters and laggards were thus selected against, and bullies lost their power to bully.

parameters.name: Leadership and dominance (no rulers; prestige by consent; exit available)
parameters.eea_baseline: Mobile hunter-gatherer bands had no rulers. Decisions that affected the group were reached by discussion toward consensus. Influence came from prestige and lasted only while others chose to listen. Anyone who tried to dominate was mocked, shunned or expelled, and in extreme cases killed. People could also leave a camp for another one, and that option checked anyone who tried to take control.
parameters.modern_default: Rulers are chosen at state scale. The people who hold power are personally unknown to almost everyone they govern, and the polity is in practice impossible to leave.
parameters.gap_statement: The forager checks on dominance (ridicule, shunning, walking away, a voice in a face-to-face decision) have no reach over rulers who never meet the people they govern. One person's say shrinks from a share of a camp consensus to one vote among millions.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (22 Nov 2026): tested many times for mobile foragers. Mobile foragers suppress would-be dominants and leaders rule by consent across the ethnographic record (Boehm 1993, ext 688; Garfield, von Rueden and Hagen 2019, ext 689); main weakness: the ethnographies differ in method and date. Singh and Glowacki 2022 (ext 756) review 34 regions and argue that sedentary, unequal non-agricultural societies also existed through the Late Pleistocene; their data are mostly sedentary Holocene societies, and they do not dispute the description of mobile foragers. The baseline describes mobile, immediate-return foragers (Woodburn 1982, ext 677). Mbendjele BaYaka mock men who hunt a lot and in effect exiled one persistent hunter; braggarts are teased, avoided and if they persist exiled (Lewis 2014, ext 848). Tsimane fishing-trip organisers rotate across households and take no more fish than others (von Rueden et al. 2014, ext 1038). Ju/'hoansi kept social, gender and political equality for decades after cash created large wealth gaps (Wiessner and Huang 2022, ext 1034). Wealth inequality itself: EEA-SOC-14.

parameters.name: Status reference group (ranked against people who know you)
parameters.eea_baseline: A forager's standing was judged by people who knew them. Daily life ran in a camp of about 30 (Hadza) inside a lifetime pool of roughly 1,000 people known by name (Ache, Hadza). The status monitor weighs this local audience most: across 15 small-scale communities (899 people), the shame people expected to feel over an act tracked how much their own community would think less of them (mean r 0.84) more closely than how other communities would (0.69). In four US studies, respect in one's face-to-face groups went with well-being more strongly than income or education did, and well-being rose and fell with that standing.
parameters.modern_default: Rank can be compared against people who will never know you: celebrities, strangers' edited lives, follower and like counts. No study in Cor measures how many people a person compares themselves with online. The measured link between social media use and low mood is small (r about 0.1 in meta-analyses of adolescents) and near zero in time-use diaries.
parameters.gap_statement: The audience that sets a person's standing grows from a group that knows them to an open-ended field of strangers whose judgement the person cannot meet or change. Hours online are not the measure (DA4): the link between time on social media and low mood is small, and the cost shows where a whole group moves onto a feed, most for students more likely to compare badly with their peers (ext 2031, 2032).
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested once. Strongest study: Sznycer et al. 2018 (ext 722), 899 people in 15 small-scale communities, none of them mobile foragers. The local-ladder paper (Anderson et al. 2012) is US students and adults from one research group. Leary 1995 (ext 621) reads the sociometer as tuned to a small set of significant others; that reading is theoretical, the studies did not compare known people with strangers. Modern side: hours on social media go with low mood weakly (ext 103, 104) and near zero in time-use diaries (ext 102); hours are not the row's measure (DA4). The gap statement rests on the staggered arrival of Facebook at 775 US colleges, where poor mental health rose most among students likely to compare badly with their peers (Braghieri, Levy and Makarin 2022, ext 2031, 2032), tested once.
