parameters.name: How standing is earned (prestige and dominance)
parameters.eea_baseline: Two routes to rank exist: dominance, through fear, and prestige, through skill that others choose to defer to. In experiments with strangers both routes work. In small-scale societies prestige is the stronger route to leadership (Chabu, Tsimane), and in mobile foragers a leader's influence is informal, tied to the situation, and rests on others choosing to follow. Authority from skill stays inside the activity: Mbendjele BaYaka specialists are consulted on elephant hunting, healing or ritual and can oblige no one, and Tsimane fishing-trip organisers rotate across households and take no extra fish. Respect is different: where it was measured (one Tsimane village of 57 men, the Chabu), fighting ability, influence and respect sat with the same few men.

eea_value.tsimane_task_leaders: only 7 of 31 regular households never organised a fishing trip (von Rueden et al. 2014)

parameters.modern_default: Standing is earned in large organisations and markets among people who mostly do not know each other, through titles, pay and audience size. Formal authority carries across domains: a manager commands in every part of the job, and wealth or fame buys influence outside the skill that earned it.
parameters.gap_statement: In the forager record, command stayed inside the activity and could be refused; modern rank carries command across domains and is hard to refuse or leave. The concentration of respect in a few people is the part that may be old: two forager-horticulturalist samples show it.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): contested. The two-routes finding is tested many times (Cheng et al. 2013, ext 622; von Rueden et al. 2011, ext 623; Garfield and Hagen 2020, ext 624). The 'authority stays inside the activity' clause holds for command in Mbendjele BaYaka ethnography (Lewis 2014) and Tsimane task leadership (von Rueden et al. 2014) and fails for respect in a Tsimane village (von Rueden et al. 2008) and among the Chabu (ext 624). Lean: holds for command, fails for respect. Both quantitative counter-samples are semi-sedentary, which leaves room for mobile bands to differ. The modern side is described, not measured here. Background-tier evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 689, 732.

parameters.name: What standing buys (children)
parameters.eea_baseline: Across 33 non-industrial societies, higher-status men had more children (meta-analysis of 288 results, overall r 0.19). The effect in foragers (Zr 0.18) was about the same as in farmers and herders. Status worked mostly through more mates and more births, less through fewer child deaths, and the effect on surviving children was about a third smaller where marriage was monogamous. Better hunters had more surviving children in five societies (Ache, Hadza, !Kung, Lamalera, Meriam). Among the Tsimane both dominance and prestige went with higher fertility, prestige most.
parameters.modern_default: In industrial societies the link between men's status and number of children is weak, and the sexes differ: men with higher incomes still have more children, mainly because poor men more often stay childless, while higher income in women and more education in both sexes typically go with fewer children (Stulp and Barrett 2016). Professional status-seeking takes the time and money that children need.
parameters.gap_statement: Status-seeking was tied to children; the motive still runs while the payoff in children has weakened or reversed. Across industrial populations, wealth, measured as income, went with higher fertility in 8 of 12 longitudinal findings, and income went with more children in men and fewer in women (Stulp and Barrett 2016); in three industrial samples the link between men's wealth and their number of children was the weakest of eleven human samples, though still positive (ext 3657), and in Britain higher-income men had more children only because low-income men were more often childless, while women's own income went with fewer children (ext 3658).
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested many times for the ancestral link, men only. Strongest study: von Rueden and Jaeggi 2016 (ext 731), 288 effects from 33 societies; weakness: very different status measures pooled, all correlational. Among the Batek, 45 years of data showed no link between foraging success or sharing and lifetime reproductive success (Kraft et al. 2019, ext 1583); with 44 adults, where the authors calculate that about 200 are needed to detect the average forager effect (ext 1584), the study was too small to test it. Two studies measured raiding: among the Waorani, men who raided more often than average did not have more wives or children (ext 897); among the Nyangatom, younger men's raiding showed no link to wives or children, while elders whom peers named as prolific raiders had more of both (ext 892). The modern link is tested: in industrial populations wealth, measured as income, went with higher fertility in 8 of 12 longitudinal findings, men's income went with more children and women's income and education with fewer (Stulp and Barrett 2016); not graded here. Background-tier evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 770, 897.

parameters.name: Wealth gaps (low to moderate in foragers)
parameters.eea_baseline: Forager material inequality was low to moderate. Weighted wealth Gini coefficients were 0.25 for hunter-gatherers and 0.27 for horticulturalists, against 0.42 for pastoralists and 0.48 for farmers, where land and livestock can be owned and inherited (21 small-scale populations). Across eleven kinds of forager wealth most Ginis fell between 0.2 and 0.5; the two material measures averaged 0.36. House sizes at 63 archaeological sites give the same order: median Gini 0.17 at hunter-gatherer sites, 0.35 at agricultural sites.
parameters.modern_default: Wealth Gini coefficients in modern states are far higher: about 0.80 for the USA in 2000 and 0.73 for China, figures Kohler et al. cite from other studies. Among the Ju/'hoansi, 44 years of cash income produced large material differences even between neighbours.
parameters.gap_statement: Wealth gaps went from small, mostly in body and skill, to very large, mostly in owned and inherited property, and the distance between top and bottom is now visible to everyone. Ju/'hoansi social and political equality held for decades after cash arrived, so a wealth gap does not by itself bring rule by the wealthy.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested many times for 'forager material inequality was low to moderate'. Independent field teams (Borgerhoff Mulder et al. 2009; Smith et al. 2010) and an independent archaeological method (Kohler et al. 2017) agree. Population limit: Tsimane, Lamalera and Meriam in the ethnographic set are not mobile foragers. The modern wealth Ginis come from Davies et al. 2011 (ext 3029, 3030): 0.801 for the USA in 2000. Ju/'hoansi change: Wiessner and Huang 2022, two communities in two countries. Background-tier evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 756.

parameters.name: Famous strangers (one-way bonds)
parameters.eea_baseline: Everyone a forager knew of could be met. The lifetime pool of individually known people was about 1,000, and the people one heard about in stories were part of the same regional network, tied to people one knew. A person you saw and heard often knew you back.
parameters.modern_default: Media supply one-way bonds with people who do not know you exist. In a quota sample of 2,028 Hungarian adults, 39% had a favourite celebrity, and on the authors' scale 4.5% of adults and 8.5% of 18 to 34 year olds had a high level of admiration. Of 151 US early adolescents, 61% thought of their favourite media figure as a relationship partner: girls mostly as a friend, boys more often as a mentor.
parameters.gap_statement: The bonding and status systems meet familiar, admired faces that never return the bond and never rank you. In a preregistered experiment, thinking about a favourite media figure lowered negative mood about as much as thinking about a friend, and did not lower loneliness, which thinking about a friend did (ext 1371); De Backer et al. 2007 read celebrity interest as learning from successful others plus mistaking celebrities for members of one's own network (argued).
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested once, for the modern prevalence (Zsila et al. 2024, one country, cut-off set by the authors; Gleason et al. 2017, one US convenience sample). The ancestral side rests on Hill et al. 2014 (ext 606-608), one model-based study in two populations. The mismatch reading is argued, not tested. Not read: Horton and Wohl 1956, Derrick et al. 2009, Kanazawa 2002. Background-tier evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 1045.

parameters.name: Size of "us" (the language group)
parameters.eea_baseline: A forager lived in a camp of a few dozen inside a wider group that shared a language and intermarried. Across 339 forager societies the regional ethnic unit had a geometric mean of about 840 people, with a wide spread (one standard deviation on the log scale runs from roughly 240 to 2,900). In 2012 the Eastern Hadza numbered about 950 people in 49 named bands sharing one language; the Ache tribe was defined by one language, had no tribe-wide leaders, and never gathered as a whole.

evidence.content: Forager residential groups vary widely in size and composition, and people moved between many groups across a regional network, so a single fixed small band is an oversimplification.
In Marlowe's cross-cultural sample of foragers, the median residential group size was 27 people (mean 41.4, range 13 to 250, across 263 societies).

parameters.name: Contact between groups (visiting and exchange alongside hostility)
parameters.eea_baseline: Forager bands were linked. Among the Hadza and Ache, adults who were in-laws or ritual partners interacted across bands more often, and in-law ties mattered about as much as blood ties. In 1974 each Ju/'hoansi adult kept about 15 gift-exchange partners living 2 to 200 km away and spent on average 4.4 months a year living with them. Humans form peaceful ties between groups, which chimpanzees do not. Hostility was also part of the record: the Ache and Hadza had hostile relations with neighbouring ethnic groups and no long-distance trade, and in 20 of 21 mobile forager societies about 15% of recorded killings were between groups.
parameters.modern_default: Contact between large groups runs through trade, media and institutions; most members of two groups never meet, marry or visit each other.
parameters.gap_statement: Forager groups were tied by marriage, visits and gifts that ran through people one knew, alongside real hostility toward some neighbours. Modern intergroup ties rarely run through personal relationships.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested once per population. Contact between bands within one language group is documented in several populations (Hill et al. 2014; Wiessner and Huang 2022, ext 752). Cor has no measured rate of marriage or trade between different language groups. Hill et al. 2014 warn that their two populations understate contact because both had hostile neighbours. Background-tier evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 672.

parameters.name: What marks someone as "them" (alliance cues)
parameters.eea_baseline: Foragers marked groups by language, dialect, ritual and marriage ties, and rarely met people genetically distant enough to look like another race. The tested part: the mind sorts people by alliance, and the sorting can be redrawn within minutes. When team membership cut across race, US participants sorted people by race less (a preregistered replication with 463 people found the drop at a smaller size; race was not erased). Arbitrary labels produce favouritism toward one's own group; a meta-analysis of cooperation experiments gives d 0.32, larger when outcomes depend on each other, and driven more by favouring 'us' than by harming 'them'.

eea_value.ingroup_favouritism_d: 0.32 overall; 0.19 bare labels; 0.42 interdependent (Balliet et al. 2014)

parameters.modern_default: Large labelled groups (parties, nations, teams) supply alliance cues without any shared life. In the US, the gap between feelings toward one's own and the other party grew from 22.64 to 40.87 points on a 0 to 100 scale between 1978 and 2016, driven by colder feelings toward the other side. The rise is not general: across 12 OECD democracies six saw it fall. Posts about the political out-group are shared more (each out-group word about 67% higher odds, US media and Congress). Sports fans claim a team's win as their own and say 'we' twice as often after a win.
parameters.gap_statement: The alliance-sorting system now runs on labels for groups of millions, with no shared life and no repeated contact, and media reward posts about 'them' (Rathje et al. 2021, eight datasets). Whether moralised posts in general spread more is contested: Brady et al. 2017 found it in 563,312 tweets, and a re-test on six other Twitter corpora gave inconsistent results (Burton, Cruz and Hahn 2021).
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested many times for 'us and them are drawn from alliance cues and can be redrawn' (Kurzban et al. 2001; Voorspoels et al. 2014 preregistered replication; Pietraszewski et al. 2014; Balliet et al. 2014 meta-analysis). parameters.name: Food shared and eaten in company
parameters.eea_baseline: In every forager group with a record, food moved between households. A review of 45 small-scale groups reports food transfers beyond the household throughout, and in all 10 groups where it was checked big game reached more families than small game. Among the Hadza of Tanzania at least 90% of the meat of large animals left the hunter's household. Among the Aka of the Congo a cook and her children ate about 20% of the stew she made, about 75% of the stew a woman ate came from other women's pots, cooking and serving were done in plain view, and the men usually ate together at the men's shelter. Among the Ju/'hoansi of Botswana each family ate the evening meal at its own fire and people then gathered at shared fires. Among the Great Andamanese game was roasted at a public cooking place and each family ate at its own hut. Batek camps in Malaysia, about 34 people, shared food at once, stored none and ate almost nothing out of camp. Hadza men ate on the foray, out of camp, about 90 percent of what they are estimated to spend in a day, most of it honey (ext 3162). The meal was mostly a family meal, eaten in sight and reach of the rest of the camp. No record shows a whole camp eating as one table every day. Sharing with the whole band was the exception and went with bands under 40 to 50 people.
parameters.modern_default: In the United States 26% of adults ate every meal of the previous day alone in 2023, more than half again above the 2003 level; among people living alone it was about 70%. In a UK poll of 2,000 adults nearly 70% had never had a meal with a neighbour. Shared meals vary widely between countries today: 11.7 lunches and dinners a week with someone known in Senegal, 2.7 in Bangladesh and Estonia. Food now comes from a shop, and a household's food does not pass through other households.
parameters.gap_statement: A forager ate food that others in the camp had caught, carried or cooked, and others ate theirs, among people who knew who gave what. A person who eats alone from a shop gets the calories without the giving and receiving. Project position: the missing exchange is what lowers mood. Among 37,193 older Japanese adults followed for three years, men living alone who usually ate alone had 2.36 times the rate of new depressive symptoms of men living alone who ate with others, after adjustment for income, health, nutrition and other factors (ext 3684); in a cross-sectional study, people who lived with their families yet ate alone had the highest odds of depressive symptoms (ext 3583).
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (19 Nov 2026): tested once for the row as a whole. That food reaches other households is tested many times: it is reported in every one of the 45 small-scale groups in Gurven's review (ext 1577). Who ate whose cooked food has been counted once. Strongest study: Kitanishi 1998 (ext 1586), 103 days of counts in two Aka camps; main weakness: one ethnographer in one region, and the 20% and 75% figures rest on his estimate of what stayed in the pot. Modern side: the US time-use series (De Neve et al. 2025, ext 1603); main weakness: one country, in a report chapter without journal review. The links between shared meals and life ratings (ext 1602, 1604) are cross-sectional and both sources leave the direction open. Sharing was also unequal and sometimes followed a demand; none of this goes against the row, since the food still moved between households among people who knew who gave what. Producers often kept more than an equal share (ext 1578), Hadza hunters' households were favoured in later data (ext 828), and Peterson argues that much sharing follows a demand (ext 709, 1580); Altman, who reports most sharing within the household, gives no counts (ext 1581), and among the Aka people avoided asking (ext 1588).

parameters.name: Who picks the partner (kin-arranged marriage)
parameters.eea_baseline: In most forager societies parents or close kin arranged marriages. In Apostolou's coding of 190 forager societies, arrangement by parents or close kin was the main way to marry in 85%, and marriage involved an exchange between the two families (brideservice, brideprice) in 80%. A phylogenetic reconstruction puts arranged marriage at least as far back as the migrations out of Africa. Courtship also existed: 3 of the 8 African forager societies in the sample marry by courtship, so the oldest African pattern is open. How much say the young people had is not coded in any source read; Hadza men and women state clear preferences for a spouse.

eea_value.arranged_primary_mode: 85% of 190 forager societies (Apostolou coding, reported by Walker et al. 2011)

parameters.modern_default: Individuals choose, and increasingly choose strangers. Among US heterosexual couples, 39% of those who met in 2017 met online, against 2% in 1995; meeting through friends fell from 33% to 20% and through family from 15% to 7%. In 2017, 89% of couples who met online had no personal connection before.
parameters.gap_statement: Partner choice moved from families and kin, who knew both people, to individuals searching alone among strangers. The people who once filtered and vouched for a partner are now mostly out of the decision.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested once. Every forager number comes from one coding of 190 societies (Apostolou 2007, ext 690, full text not read); Walker et al. 2011 reuses that coding. The modern side is US only, two nationally representative surveys from one research group (Rosenfeld et al. 2019). Background-tier evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 690, 692. Added 19 Nov 2026. Among the Tsimane of Bolivia a father helped get the spouse in 36% of 622 marriages and the preferred partner is a cross-cousin (ext 1732). In 15 of 16 historical farming states parents chose the spouse (Apostolou 2012, ext 1737). Hadza marriages are typically not arranged, by Marlowe's ethnography as cited by Sorokowski et al. 2017 (ext 1735). No source read codes a part for the camp beyond kin. On the modern side, US couples who met online broke up no more often than couples who met offline (Rosenfeld 2017, ext 1740), and marriages begun online were slightly less likely to end in a sample paid for by a dating company (ext 1741, abstract only). parameters.name: The pool of possible partners
parameters.eea_baseline: A forager chose from a small pool of people who were known before anything started. Among the Aka, the area a person explores over a lifetime, looking for a mate, visiting kin and hunting, reaches about 50 km (half the places an Aka adult has visited lie within 30 km of camp, ext 3204) and holds about 700 people they can meet and get to know. The lifetime pool of individually known people was about 1,000 in the Ache and Hadza. Possible partners came with a known family and a reputation.
parameters.modern_default: Online, the pool is effectively unbounded and made of strangers. On one large US dating site, attention was very unequal: most users got a handful of first messages at most while a few got hundreds (one woman in New York got 1,504 in a month). Men and women mostly wrote to people about 25% more desirable than themselves, and men writing to more desirable women got replies at most 21% of the time.
parameters.gap_statement: The pool grew from hundreds of known people to an open-ended list of strangers judged from a profile. Attention concentrates on a few, and most people's approaches go unanswered.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested once. parameters.name: Marriage system (mostly monogamous, some polygyny, serial pairs)
parameters.eea_baseline: Most societies in the ethnographic record permitted a man more than one wife (about 85%), but in forager societies most marriages were monogamous. In 87% of 190 forager societies fewer than 20% of men were married polygynously; among tropical African foragers polygyny runs from 3% to 20%; among Savanna Pume foragers 11% of men and 20% of women are ever married polygynously. Men contributing more food went with more monogamy. Serial pairing was common: among the !Kung and Ache, men and women had children with more than one partner.
parameters.modern_default: Law imposes one spouse at a time in most states (Japan from 1880, China 1953, India 1955, Nepal 1963). Serial pairing through divorce and new partners continues.
parameters.gap_statement: Small gap. Forager practice was already mostly one spouse at a time with some polygyny and remarriage; modern law removes the polygynous minority. Forager marriages often ended: across ten forager and forager-farmer populations reported divorce rates run from 18% (Agta) to nearly every couple (north Alaskan Inuit), and the reviewers put the general level at a quarter to a third of marriages or more, with remarriage common (ext 1728). The rates were counted differently in each population, so they cannot be averaged or set against a modern rate.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested many times for 'mostly monogamous with some polygyny in foragers' (Apostolou coding via Walker et al. 2011; Pume demography, Schacht and Kramer 2019; African forager ethnographies via Henrich et al. 2012; Marlowe 2003, ext 767). Any single number is one study. Keep 'permitted' (85% of societies) apart from 'practised' (a minority of forager marriages). Background-tier evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 767, 768. Divorce and number of mates, added 19 Nov 2026: Hewlett et al. 2023 (ext 1728, 1729) and Winking and Gurven 2011 (ext 1730) compile the original demographic studies; main weakness: each team counted divorce differently.

parameters.name: Number of children and spacing
parameters.eea_baseline: Forager women who lived through their reproductive years had about six births: Ache 8.2, Agta 6.9, Hadza 6.2, Hiwi 5.5, Ju/'hoansi 4.3; the mean across 75 natural-fertility societies was 5.98. Births were spaced about 3 to 4 years apart (hunter-gatherer average 3.7 years). About a third of forager women survived to complete their fertility. With pregnancy and long breastfeeding, menstrual cycles were few: among the Dogon, natural-fertility farmers, a woman had about 100 menstruations in her life.
parameters.modern_default: World births per woman fell from 4.84 in 1950 to 2.23 in 2021, and fell in every country. A US woman with three births has about three times the Dogon count of menstruations.
parameters.gap_statement: Fewer children, fewer pregnancies and far more menstrual cycles. Each birth lowered the relative risk of breast cancer by 7.0 percent and each 12 months of breastfeeding by a further 4.3 percent across 47 studies in 30 countries, and the authors estimate that the births and breastfeeding usual in developing countries until recently would cut the cumulative risk by age 70 in developed countries from 6.3 to 2.7 per 100 women (Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer 2002). Women in the top quarter of lifetime ovulatory cycles had 1.81 times the odds of ovarian cancer of women in the bottom quarter (Pelucchi et al. 2007). Childlessness at 10 to 20% is high, but it is no new level for Europe. No forager source on the share of adults who never reproduce was found.

parameters.name: What gets a person chosen, and how unequal men are
parameters.eea_baseline: Among foragers, men who hunted better had more surviving children (Ache, Hadza, !Kung, Lamalera, Meriam), and Hadza men with deeper voices and stronger upper bodies had more children. Hadza women put great weight on a man's foraging, and men on a woman working hard. Men's number of children varied more than women's: the male to female variance ratio was 1.66 among the Aka, 1.77 among the !Kung, 1.93 among the Hadza and 4.22 among the Ache. How large the gap is depends on the marriage system; in monogamous populations it is about 1.
parameters.modern_default: Stated preferences keep the same sex differences across 45 countries (14,399 people): men weight looks and youth more, women earning prospects and an older partner. On dating sites attention concentrates on a few. In the US, the share of men aged 18 to 24 with no sex in the past year rose from 18.9% (2000 to 2002) to 30.9% (2016 to 2018), and men with lower income and no full-time work were more often sexually inactive.
parameters.gap_statement: Choice used to run on skill and character seen over years in a small group. On apps it runs on photos and stated traits, and stated preferences barely predict whom people like when they meet. Whether the rise in sexless young men comes from this shift is untested.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested many times that good hunters and high-status men had more children (ext 770, ext 731) and that male variance in reproductive success is higher on average (Brown et al. 2009, 18 populations). The size of the sex gap varies with the marriage system (Brown et al. 2009, ext 1003), as the baseline states. Stated preferences barely predict whom people like when they meet (Eastwick et al. 2014, ext 757), as the gap statement states. parameters.name: Alloparental care supply (a village, not a dyad)
parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral human infants were not raised by a mother alone but by a network of allomothers - fathers, grandmothers, aunts, older siblings, and trusted non-kin - who shared both direct care (holding, carrying, soothing) and provisioning (food). Humans are a cooperatively breeding ape: unlike other African apes, whose mothers nurture infants essentially on their own, hominin mothers relied on groupmates to protect, care for, and provision their unusually slow-maturing, costly young. This was not a cultural add-on but species architecture: a human child requires on the order of 13 million calories from birth to independence, and humans breed faster (every 3-4 years) than chimpanzees and orangutans (about every 5.5 and 7.7 years; gorillas breed about every 3.8 years, Galdikas and Wood 1990, ext 3519) while producing larger, slower-maturing babies - a life-history paradox solvable only by shared provisioning. Across foraging ethnography, infants were routinely handled by people other than the mother from shortly after birth: among the Hadza, the mother does roughly 69% of the time children aged four and under were held (ext 2128) and allomothers the rest; !Kung infants have the mother's entire social world available with intense face-to-face engagement; Trobriand infants are suckled by lactating allomothers. The infant's evolved expectation is a reliable surround of multiple invested caregivers, not a single isolated dyad.

eea_value.note: Specific aggregate 'alloparent count ~4+' and a generic '40-50% of care delivered by allomothers' figure are widely cited in the literature but are NOT verbatim-grounded in Cor's extractions; only the Hadza ~69/31 mother/allomother holding split and the qualitative multi-caregiver pattern are. Numbers given are the extraction-supported anchors, not an asserted universal mean.

parameters.modern_default: The modern default is the isolated nuclear (often single-caregiver) household: one or two adults, frequently without resident grandmothers, aunts, older cousins, or trusted neighbours sharing the daily load. The idealized breadwinner-father / homemaker-mother / biological-children unit is a historical aberration roughly a century old (Victorian at most; the 1950s template in the US), departing from the extended-kin allomaternal norm that held for the vast majority of human history. Care that was distributed across many hands is now concentrated on one or two, often supplemented by paid, rotating, or institutional caregivers rather than a stable invested kin network.
parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is between the reliable, present, multi-caregiver surround the infant's attachment and the mother's reproductive psychology evolved to expect, and the thin one- or two-adult household the modern environment supplies. The load that was carried by a village now falls on isolated parents; maternal investment is calibrated to assess available allomaternal support (M9), so its evolved absence produces overload, depleted caregivers, and infants with fewer attachment figures than the cooperative-breeding design assumes. This is a supply mismatch, not a parental-competence failure.
parameters.resolution_unit: Reliable, present alloparental supply - care plus provisioning actually delivered by invested caregivers - NOT bare kin count or genealogical presence. Four relatives who live far away and do not share the daily load do not satisfy the parameter; what the infant and mother expect is dependable, hands-on, repeated care from a stable surround.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Shared infant care is observed in many forager populations by separate field teams (Hadza, Efe, Aka, !Kung, Agta, Pume); the share of care varies widely. The 'cooperative breeder' reading and the calorie argument stay Hrdy's interpretation. In 15,696 UK infants, care by kin (odds ratio 0.61) and formal daycare (0.68) as the main weekday care went with lower odds of developmental delay at 9 months, and an infant whose mother had none of the six kinds of help and company measured (care by kin in working hours, seeing her own mother, time with friends, other mothers to talk to, family she could count on for money, people at the birth) had about eight times the odds of delay of one whose mother had the most of all six (Waynforth 2024).

parameters.name: Caregiver continuity and reliability (present, not merely countable)
parameters.eea_baseline: The ancestral infant developed within a web of stable, repeatedly-present attachment figures whose availability could be counted on. Attachment is not a single dyadic bond but secure attachment to one or more trusted caretakers - Bowlby's design refined by Hrdy to plural, reliably-present figures - and human infants are equipped with traits (cuteness, prolonged eye contact, social smiling, differentiated cries) for recruiting and holding the attention of multiple potential caretakers. Crucially, maternal commitment itself is contingent and reliability-sensitive: for a cooperatively breeding mammal, the capacity to conceive is only part of the equation; the mother must be able to carry through to rearing independence, which she assesses against the dependable support actually available. Touch is part of this continuity - the infant evolved to expect near-continuous skin contact (carried, held, co-sleeping), a sense developed first in utero and serving as a primary regulatory channel. The expectation is not a list of relatives but caregivers who are reliably, physically present across time.
parameters.modern_default: Modern caregiving is frequently discontinuous and rotating: paid daycare with staff turnover, sequential and inconsistent caregivers, geographically dispersed or intermittently-available kin, and reduced continuous body contact (separate sleeping, stroller and crib time, scheduled rather than on-demand holding). Caregivers may be nominally present (counted on paper) yet not reliably, responsively available in the moment-to-moment way the regulatory system expects.
parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is between caregiver reliability/continuity as an experienced, present regulatory input and a modern environment that often supplies caregivers who are countable but not dependably present. Because maternal investment and infant attachment are both calibrated to perceived caregiver reliability (M9, R1), low continuity is not neutral: it degrades the secure-base scaffolding and the touch-mediated regulation the infant evolved to expect, even when the number of caregivers on paper looks adequate.
parameters.resolution_unit: Reliable, present caregiver supply - responsive caregivers actually and repeatedly available across time, including continuity of body contact - NOT a count of designated or genealogically-related caregivers. The naive reading (enough named caregivers exist) misleads; what regulates the infant is dependable presence.
parameters.confidence_note: All supporting extractions for the continuity/reliability claim are graded theoretical (Hrdy/Bowlby interpretive synthesis); the touch items are 296 (theoretical) and 294 (cross_species, Harlow/Suomi). The row is graded argued, not yet tested. The claim that maternal commitment is contingent on perceived reliable support (281, 402) and that attachment is to plural trusted figures (276) is well-grounded; the specific operationalization of 'continuity' as a measured construct is not pinned to a number, hence eea_value is null and the parameter is qualitative.

parameters.name: Mixed-age child playgroups as developmental input
parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral children developed social competence largely through self-organized, free, physically-active play with a mixed-age band of other children - younger and older mixed together - rather than under continuous adult supervision or in age-segregated peer cohorts. Rough-and-tumble and pretend play during the juvenile period is a dedicated developmental input: in the mammalian design, play is a distinct emotional system (Panksepp's PLAY) and play experience physically tunes the maturing prefrontal cortex, refining the circuits that later dampen the amygdala and support social reciprocity, partner discrimination, and emotional regulation. Critically, the AMOUNT and quality of play partners matters: animals raised with more play partners show progressively greater play experience and corresponding PFC development, and even the untreated playmates of more-playful partners develop greater cortical thickness - play is a partnered input, so a richer multi-partner (and, in the human case, multi-age) play environment is the expected calibrating stimulus.
parameters.modern_default: Modern childhood compresses or eliminates free mixed-age play: age-segregated grade cohorts and daycare, adult-structured and supervised activities, indoor screen-based leisure, reduced unsupervised outdoor roaming, and safety norms that discourage rough-and-tumble. Children spend far less time in self-directed, physically-active, mixed-age peer play than the developmental window evolved to expect.
parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is between mixed-age, self-organized, physically-active play as the evolved calibrating input for the juvenile prefrontal cortex (M4, embedded in the alloparental child-minding network, M9) and a modern environment that supplies age-segregated, adult-structured, often sedentary substitutes. In rats, play with partners shapes the developing cortex (Pellis & Pellis 2009, ext 212, 220). Cor reads reduced free play in children as a missing developmental input. In children, general risky outdoor play (13 studies) and places that allow risky play (21 studies) went with better physical, mental, social and cognitive outcomes in a review of 74 studies (Ramsden et al. 2026), and children who played adventurously more had slightly fewer internalising symptoms and more positive affect (Dodd, Nesbit and FitzGibbon 2023).
parameters.resolution_unit: Self-directed, mixed-age, physically-active free play actually engaged in - partnered play experience - NOT adult-structured activities, solitary screen play, or scheduled lessons that occupy time without delivering the rough-and-tumble, role-reversal, peer-negotiated input the circuits expect.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Mixed-age child playgroups are documented across forager societies in two systematic reviews (Lew-Levy et al. 2017, 2018). The label covers the ancestral value only: the claim that age mixing shapes development rests on rat work and is untested in humans. In monkeys, isolates recovered with younger partners (ext 542). A review of tests of pretend play found weak and inconsistent evidence that it causes the developmental gains credited to it (Lillard et al. 2013, ext 762); the tests it reviews are mostly adult-led play training in preschools, which is not the self-organised play this row describes.

parameters.name: Multigenerational presence (older people inside the band's giving and getting)
parameters.eea_baseline: Older people kept a place in the band's giving and getting. They gave food, care and knowledge where they could, and they were given to. Project position (21 Nov 2026): reciprocity runs across the whole life, so a grandmother who gave for a lifetime holds her place when she takes. What older people gave differed by group. Among the Hadza, grandmothers foraged most when their newest grandchild was youngest (ext 2063). Among the Tsimane, net food flowed down the generations: grandmothers gave a net 117 kcal a day to their grandchildren and grandfathers 223, into their 70s (ext 3088). Among the Aka, care by others, largely grandmothers, lowered mothers' work by up to 216 kcal over nine hours (ext 2084). Tsimane adults named grandparents most often as the source of the stories they knew (ext 3827). Among the Ache and Hiwi, older women did not contribute food that eased the deficits of middle-aged couples raising children, and about 10 percent of middle-aged Ache women lived with their own mothers (ext 2301). Agta adults named old age among the needs that decided whom they gave to in an experimental sharing game (ext 3665). Human longevity itself is bound up with this role: the grandmother hypothesis (and Lieberman's active-grandparent corollary) holds that the long human life after the last birth (among 52 wild mammal species found only in humans, orcas and short-finned pilot whales, ext 3722) was selected for and made possible by older adults remaining physically active to help rear children, grandchildren, and other young kin, increasing inclusive fitness through kin-selected provisioning. Older people are thus part of the alloparental supply: a band of several generations in which the old kept a place in the exchange and were no absent generation.
parameters.modern_default: Modern households are frequently bi-generational or single-generation: grandparents commonly live separately, often at a geographic distance, outside the family's daily giving and getting. In ten European countries 58 percent of grandmothers and 49 percent of grandfathers looked after a grandchild in the past year (Hank and Buber 2009, ext 4209). Where grandparents are present they are often less physically active and less part of the family's daily life than in a band of several generations.
parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is between older people who keep a place in the daily giving and getting of a band of several generations (M9, M3) and the modern default of grandparents who live apart from it. What they gave to the rearing of the young, in food, care and knowledge, and what was given back to them, is missing for many modern families, which thins the network of carers.
parameters.resolution_unit: Older relatives present and inside the family's daily giving and getting: giving care, food or knowledge where they can, and being provided for. NOT mere grandparental existence or living-relative count. A surviving grandmother several time zones away does not fill the place a band of several generations gave her.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (22 Nov 2026): tested many times for what the row claims, that older people were present and inside the giving and getting. Post-reproductive survival is common across foragers (Gurven and Kaplan 2007, ext 723), and food and care from older people were measured by separate teams among the Hadza (ext 2063), the Tsimane (ext 3088) and the Aka (ext 2084); main weakness: each flow is measured in one population, and among the Ache and Hiwi older women did not ease the deficits of middle-aged couples (ext 2301). The grandmother hypothesis in the baseline is an evolutionary reading, which the label does not cover; on child survival, across 17 patrilineal populations surviving maternal grandparents went with lower child mortality and paternal grandparents did not (Strassmann and Garrard 2011, ext 3536). On child growth, among 127 Aka children grandmothers were the allomother most linked to better nutritional status, clearest from 9 months to 3 years (Meehan, Helfrecht and Quinlan 2014). On food the row states a project position (21 Nov 2026): a grandmother who gave for a lifetime need not feed anyone to hold her place. Measured flows differ by group: down the generations among the Tsimane (ext 3088); Hadza grandmothers foraged more when grandchildren were youngest (ext 2063); among the Ache and Hiwi older women did not ease the deficits of middle-aged couples (ext 2301).

evidence.author_quote: In order to elucidate the links between exercise and aging, I propose a corollary to the grandmother hypothesis, which I call the active grandparent hypothesis. According to this idea, human longevity was not only selected for but also made possible by having to work moderately during old age to help as many children, grandchildren, and other younger relatives as possible to survive and thrive. That is, while there might have been selection for genes (as yet unidentified) that help humans live past the age of fifty, there was also selection for genes that repair and maintain our bodies when we are physically active. As a result, many of the mechanisms that slow aging and extend life are turned on by physical activity, especially as we get older. Human health and longevity are thus extended both by and for physical activity.

parameters.name: Affective (C-tactile) contact frequency and skin-to-skin time
parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral infants and children lived in near-continuous bodily contact: carried on the body, fed at short intervals, and held skin-to-skin for much of the day and night, with frequent affectionate, moderate-pressure touch from the mother and a wider circle of caregivers. Adults likewise lived in high-touch social fields where casual physical contact was a routine, primary channel of social interaction. Touch is the phylogenetically first and largest sense organ; the fetus is already continuously stimulated in utero. Skin-to-skin/carried contact was the species-typical default, not an intervention.

eea_value.note: No defensible single ancestral 'touches-per-hour' number; cross-cultural touch frequency ranges enormously (0-180+ contacts/hour across modern societies per Jourard), so the EEA value is a high-contact regime with a floor, not a point estimate
eea_value.infant_contact: near-continuous (carried, co-sleeping, fed at frequent short intervals)
eea_value.caregiver_scope: mother plus alloparents; high-touch social field for adults

parameters.modern_default: WEIRD/industrialized environments are historically unusual in touch avoidance: infants spend much time in cribs, strollers, and carriers that minimize skin contact; personal-space norms and screen-mediated interaction strip casual affective touch from daily adult life. Many people experience chronic 'touch hunger' below the developmental and regulatory floor.
parameters.gap_statement: Modern environments routinely fall below the ancestral affective-touch floor. Touch deprivation in extreme cases (institutional rearing) produces growth-hormone suppression, immune dysfunction, and developmental arrest; even in non-extreme modern life the loss of moderate-pressure affective touch removes a direct oxytocin/vagal/cortisol-regulating input. Critically, affective touch is the one ancestral channel that remote, volumetric, or screen-based technology cannot deliver: it requires physical skin contact.
parameters.resolution_unit: Reliable supply of moderate-pressure, skin-to-skin/affective (C-tactile) contact, especially in infancy and under stress; NOT incidental or light/ticklish touch (light touch does not produce the physiological response) and NOT a raw count of any contact.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Near-continuous infant carrying and frequent nursing are documented in !Kung, Aka and Efe, with breastfeeding into the second or third year across non-industrial societies (Sellen 2007). parameters.name: Co-sleeping / nighttime body contact
parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral infants and young children slept in body contact with the mother and others rather than alone, extending the daytime carried-contact regime through the night. Nighttime proximity meant the touch, warmth, and physiological co-regulation channels (and likely circadian entrainment cues from the caregiver) operated continuously across the 24-hour cycle, not just during waking.
parameters.modern_default: WEIRD norms favor solitary infant sleep in a separate crib or room, removing nighttime body contact for most of the sleep period; adult sleep is also frequently solitary or contact-minimized.
parameters.gap_statement: Solitary infant and child sleep removes the nighttime half of the ancestral continuous-contact regime, eliminating touch-based physiological co-regulation during sleep. The evidence that night contact regulates infant physiology comes from one lab (McKenna 2014, ext 615, 616).
parameters.resolution_unit: Reliable presence of nighttime body contact / proximity that preserves the touch and co-regulation channel through the sleep period; the relevant variable is continuity of contact across the 24-hour cycle, not sleep duration.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Mother and infant slept in the same room in all 173 societies of the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample and in the same bed in at least 76 (Barry and Paxson 1971). The label covers that ancestral fact only. It says nothing about the safety of bed-sharing today: the AAP 2016 guidance (room-sharing without bed-sharing) stands. The two largest case-control analyses disagree on bed-sharing where no other hazard is present: Blair et al. 2014 found no significant added risk (odds ratio 1.1), with about 18 times the risk on a sofa or beside an adult who had drunk alcohol (ext 3346); Carpenter et al. 2013 found about five times the risk for breastfed babies under 3 months whose parents neither smoke nor drink (ext 3347). parameters.name: Affective grooming/touch from trusted others (adult social touch)
parameters.eea_baseline: Beyond infancy, ancestral adults maintained social bonds through frequent affiliative body contact: the human homolog of primate grooming. Ancestral adults lived in high-touch social fields where reassuring, stress-buffering touch from trusted others (partners, kin, allies) was a routine, ever-present channel of social and physiological regulation.

parameters.name: Dawn/dusk light gradient with genuine nocturnal darkness as circadian entrainment signal
parameters.eea_baseline: Across evolutionary history the human circadian pacemaker (suprachiasmatic nucleus) was entrained by a high-amplitude natural light-dark cycle: bright full-spectrum daytime illumination (often >10,000 lux outdoors), a gradual dusk dimming and reddening, and then real darkness for the duration of the biological night, with only firelight (low, long-wavelength) as evening illumination. Contemporary hunter-gatherer reference populations (Hadza, San) show sleep onset clustering around 8-10 p.m., aligned with dusk-driven melatonin release. The operative signal is the timing and spectral content of light at the day-night transition reaching melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells, not light intensity per se.
parameters.modern_default: Indoor electric and screen light keeps evening illumination bright and short-wavelength (blue-enriched, ~450nm) well past dusk, suppressing melatonin and delaying its onset by 1.5-3 hours; daytime indoor light is far dimmer than outdoor light, flattening the day-night amplitude. The dusk dimming/reddening gradient and true nocturnal darkness are largely abolished.
parameters.gap_statement: The modern light environment inverts the ancestral pattern on both ends: too little bright light by day, too much blue-enriched light at night, with no real darkness. This delays circadian phase, compresses and fragments the biological night, and decouples internal time from external solar time.
parameters.resolution_unit: Spectral timing of light exposure at the day-night transition (dusk dimming + nocturnal darkness), not total daily light dose or generic 'brightness'.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Pre-electric light exposure and sleep timing are measured in Hadza, San and Tsimane (Yetish et al. 2015), in Toba/Qom with and without electricity (de la Iglesia et al. 2015) and in natural-light camping studies; samples are small and modern foragers stand in for ancestral ones. Sleep onset averaged about 3.3 hours after sunset in Yetish et al. In about 400,000 UK adults, each extra hour a day outdoors in daylight went with less frequent low mood and tiredness, fewer insomnia symptoms, an earlier chronotype and lower odds of antidepressant use (Burns et al. 2021).

parameters.name: Sleep timing/phase alignment to the biological night (not a fixed duration target)
parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestrally, sleep occurred within a stable phase relationship to the solar/circadian night: onset about three hours after sunset (3.3 hours on average among Hadza, San and Tsimane, ext 2224; about three hours in rural Haiti without electricity, ext 3903), offset near or before dawn, with the sleep episode anchored to internal circadian time. Field data from three preindustrial societies (Hadza, San, Tsimane) place habitual sleep within a window in the rough range of ~6-7 hours of nocturnal sleep; subsistence horticulturalists on Tanna, Vanuatu, slept about 7.4 to 7.9 hours (ext 2813), but the load-bearing ancestral feature is the alignment of the sleep episode to circadian phase, not hitting a particular hour count. Total nightly sleep duration in such groups is modest and overlaps the lower end of modern recommendations; there is no evidence of a hard-wired 8-9 hour requirement.
parameters.modern_default: Industrial schedules set wake (and increasingly sleep) times by clock and alarm rather than by internal time, producing chronic 'social jetlag' - a standing offset between the endogenous circadian phase and the socially imposed sleep window. In a large Central-European dataset ~69% experience >=1 hour of social jetlag and about one-third >=2 hours; ~80% of workers wake by alarm; population chronotype has drifted later while workday sleep has shortened.
parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is primarily one of phase, not amount. Even when total sleep is adequate, misalignment between biological and social clocks is associated with metabolic harm (e.g. social jetlag raises overweight odds and predicts BMI in the overweight, with an effect more than half that of sleep duration, after controlling for duration itself). Across 43 studies of 231,648 people, social jetlag went with higher body mass index and 1.2 times the odds of overweight (Arab et al. 2024), and in the high-quality studies of a review of 68 with higher body mass index, waist, systolic blood pressure and HbA1c (Bouman et al. 2023). In 60,977 UK adults, regular sleep and wake times predicted lower mortality more strongly than sleep duration did (Windred et al. 2024). Chasing a duration number while ignoring phase misses the operative variable.
parameters.resolution_unit: Sleep timing/phase - the alignment of the sleep episode to internal circadian night - NOT sleep duration.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Night-anchored sleep of about 5.7 to 7.1 hours is measured by actigraphy in three forager societies (Yetish et al. 2015), in 33 Hadza adults across 393 days of recording in all (6.25 hours a night, with stronger circadian rhythms than Western populations; Samson et al. 2017) and in Toba/Qom (de la Iglesia et al. 2015); camping studies move phase while duration holds. Actigraphy only, and parts of the interpretation are disputed. The two camping experiments (Wright et al. 2013, ext 610; Stothard et al. 2017, ext 613) come from the same laboratory and share authors.

parameters.name: Falling evening ambient temperature as a second sleep-onset cue
parameters.eea_baseline: Outside thermally buffered shelter, ancestral evenings carried a reliable nocturnal drop in ambient temperature that paralleled dusk. This descending thermal ramp coincides with the endogenous evening fall in core body temperature that gates sleep onset, plausibly acting as a second zeitgeber-like onset cue alongside light. The baseline environment thus paired a dimming light gradient with a falling temperature gradient at the day-night transition.
parameters.modern_default: Climate-controlled indoor environments hold ambient temperature roughly constant across the 24-hour cycle, removing the evening cooling ramp; evening heat (and sometimes overheated bedrooms) can also oppose the core-temperature fall required for sleep onset.
parameters.gap_statement: By flattening the daily thermal cycle, modern housing removes a candidate onset cue that historically co-occurred with dusk and reinforced circadian timing, potentially leaving light as the sole (and now corrupted) entrainment channel.
parameters.resolution_unit: Direction and timing of the evening ambient-temperature change (a falling ramp at dusk), not absolute thermostat setpoint or daytime comfort.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested once. Yetish et al. 2015 found sleep fell during the nightly drop in ambient temperature in Hadza, San and Tsimane; one research group, association only. That temperature acts as a sleep cue is argued.

parameters.name: Daily incidental movement load
parameters.eea_baseline: Across a foraging day, adults covered substantial ground on foot as a structural side-effect of acquiring food, water, and firewood and of moving between patches and camp: Hadza men walk about 11.4 km a day and women about 5.8 km, and the women also dig for several hours (Pontzer et al. 2012, GPS; ext 196). Movement was woven through the whole waking day rather than concentrated into a bout. Activity was modest in intensity but near-continuous and embedded: light chores, child-carrying, frequent sit-to-stand transitions, and active resting postures (squatting, kneeling, ground-sitting) that sustain low-level lower-limb muscle activity. Hunter-gatherer PAL is only modestly above a Western desk worker's (~1.8-1.9 vs ~1.6), so the EEA baseline is not 'extreme exertion' but 'movement is the unavoidable medium of subsistence.'

daily_distance_km.source: Pontzer et al. 2012, PLoS ONE, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0040503 (GPS means)
daily_distance_km.qualifier: Hadza only; a side effect of the foraging day

rest_hours_per_day.note: comparable to industrialized adults; difference is posture not amount

parameters.modern_default: Movement has been extracted from subsistence and re-inserted, if at all, as discretionary 'exercise': set-aside, planned, dose-prescribed (e.g. 150 min/week guidelines), and separated from the rest of a chair-bound, motor-transported, indoor day. Most waking hours are spent in continuous chair-sitting that holds the lower limbs near-inactive, and total daily distance on foot collapses far below the ancestral range.
parameters.gap_statement: The gap is not a calorie or PAL gap (these are surprisingly close) but a distributional one: ancestral movement was low-intensity, continuous, and obligatory; modern movement is optional, bunched, and easily skipped, leaving long uninterrupted muscular-inactivity bouts that the body never encountered. The mismatch is in HOW the day's muscle activity is spread, not in gross energy turnover.
parameters.resolution_unit: Incidental all-day movement woven into the fabric of living (errands, carrying, standing, walking between activities, active rest postures) - NOT a set-aside 'exercise' session. The functional target is the continuous distribution of low-level activity across waking hours, not weekly minutes of vigorous training.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Forager activity of over 100 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous movement and activity levels modestly above Western ones are found across populations (Pontzer, Wood and Raichlen 2018); the kilometre and rest figures are Hadza only.

Although these few hours of hustling and bustling per day make them about twelve times more active than the average American or European, by no stretch of the imagination could one characterize their workloads as backbreaking. On average, the women walk five miles a day and dig for several hours, whereas the men walk between seven and ten miles a day. And when they aren't being very active, they typically rest or do light work.

I didn't realize I had walked into a camp until I found myself amid about fifteen Hadza men, women, and children who were sitting on the ground as shown in figure 2. parameters.name: Effort-to-outcome contingency (closed-loop, self-attributable)
parameters.eea_baseline: Subsistence effort sat in a short, visible, self-attributable causal loop: the same individual who tracked, dug, gathered, knapped, or built directly observed the outcome of that effort, on a timescale of minutes to days. Effort-outcome links were embodied and legible - you could see whether your action produced the result. The evolved controllability circuitry (vmPFC detects response-outcome contingency and, when contingency is present, inhibits the dorsal-raphe passivity default) was calibrated to environments where such contingency was routinely present and detectable, and where experiences of control immunized against later helplessness.
parameters.modern_default: Much modern productive effort is decoupled from any visible, self-attributable outcome: work is mediated by long opaque chains, algorithmic management, and electronic monitoring that reduce decision latitude; rewards are detached in time and attribution from the effort that earned them; and many roles offer high demand with low control. The closed loop between one's own action and an observable result is frequently broken.
parameters.gap_statement: Because passivity is the unlearned default that only switches OFF when controllability is detected, environments that obscure the effort-outcome link don't feel neutral - they default the organism toward helplessness-type physiology. The gap is the loss of routinely detectable, self-attributable contingency, which population health data link to elevated disease risk (low job control predicts coronary disease independent of grade).
parameters.resolution_unit: Reliably PRESENT and DETECTABLE response-outcome contingency that the actor can attribute to their own effort - not mere busyness, throughput, or nominal 'autonomy.' What must be restored is the closed, legible loop between action and observed result, not the quantity of work.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): argued, not yet tested. No study measures how visible the link between effort and outcome was in forager work; the ancestral claim is a mismatch synthesis (van Vugt et al. 2024). The Whitehall II and rodent controllability findings test the modern side and the mechanism, not this ancestral value.

parameters.name: Task diversity within the subsistence day
parameters.eea_baseline: A forager's day cycled through a wide and shifting portfolio of tasks - tracking, gathering, digging, processing, toolmaking/repair, child-tending, food sharing, travel - recruiting varied skills and continually engaging the appetitive SEEKING/exploration system across novel and changing problems. The evolved exploratory-pursuit substrate (mesolimbic-dopamine SEEKING) is built for persistent inquisitive engagement with a varied environment, not for indefinitely repeating one narrow operation.
parameters.modern_default: Industrial and much digital work narrows the day to repetitive, specialized, often single-task operation - high repetition, low task variety, minimal novel problem-solving - with the SEEKING system left chronically under-stimulated by the work itself and frequently redirected onto engineered supernormal substitutes (feeds, games, variable-ratio rewards) off the clock.
parameters.gap_statement: The gap is the collapse from a high-variety, skill-diverse subsistence portfolio to narrow repetitive specialization, under-engaging the exploratory-pursuit system whose canonical evolved function is varied engagement with a changing world. No study in Cor measures forager task diversity.
parameters.resolution_unit: Genuine variety of self-directed, skill-recruiting tasks across the day that engage exploration and problem-solving - not nominal 'multitasking' (rapid switching among equally shallow operations) and not enrichment proxies bolted on outside the core work.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade: argued, not yet tested. Van Vugt et al. 2024 describe ancestral work as small-group, embodied, skill-based and autonomy-rich (ext 583). They do not measure task diversity. The substrate is Panksepp's SEEKING system (ext 251, 397). No study in Cor links task variety itself to health or mood.

parameters.name: Daily subsistence work-hours (contested)
parameters.eea_baseline: No daily work-hour figure is settled. The 'original affluent society' position (Sahlins/Lee) reads the data as short food-quest hours and ample leisure; the opposing reading (Kaplan/Hawkes/Pontzer, and Lieberman's own qualifications) emphasizes that total productive effort includes processing, childcare, toolwork, and travel, and that activity is modest-intensity but spread across the day. What the full-text evidence DOES support qualitatively is that forager workloads are not 'backbreaking' and that overall energetic activity is only modestly above a sedentary Westerner's - but this does not license any specific daily work-hour figure.
parameters.modern_default: Modern work is organized around fixed, externally scheduled, often long and boundary-less hours (clock-time labor, always-on digital availability) - a structurally different time-architecture from intermittent, self-paced, weather- and resource-contingent subsistence effort, regardless of what the ancestral hour-count actually was.
parameters.gap_statement: The defensible mismatch is in the STRUCTURE of work-time (externally clocked, continuous, boundary-less vs. intermittent, self-paced, contingent), not in any claimed reduction or increase in daily hours.
parameters.resolution_unit: Self-paced, resource-contingent, intermittently-bounded work time - the time ARCHITECTURE (when and how effort is scheduled and bounded), not a target number of daily hours.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): contested. Weight of evidence: once processing, travel and childcare are counted, forager work time is longer than the short-hours figures, while foragers still have more leisure than neighbouring farmers (Dyble et al. 2019); no single daily hour figure is supported.

evidence.author_quote: When Herman Pontzer and his colleagues measured daily energy expenditures in the Hadza, they were surprised to find that the highly active Hadza spend about the same total number of calories per day as sedentary industrialized people with the same lean body weight. In addition, when Pontzer and colleagues collected energetic data from adults in many countries including the United States, Ghana, Jamaica, and South Africa, they observed that more active people spent only slightly more calories per day than more sedentary people who weighed the same. In addition, individuals who were more physically active didn't have total energy budgets as high as their exertions would predict. How could someone who spent five hundred extra calories a day exercising not have a total energy budget that is five hundred calories higher? The proposed explanation is that people's total energy budgets are constrained: if I use five hundred extra calories walking, I'll spend less energy on my resting metabolism to help pay for my exertions.

parameters.name: Food diversity and seasonality (whole-food, micronutrient-dense, omnivorous variety)
parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral intake came from a wide, seasonally rotating array of wild plant and animal foods eaten in their whole, minimally altered form. Diet composition shifted with paleontological period, geography, and season, sustaining the broad versatility typical of an omnivore. Macronutrient and micronutrient profiles diverged sharply from the modern Western diet in nearly every measurable dimension at once: higher protein share, dramatically less refined carbohydrate and added sugar, lower sodium, higher potassium, higher micronutrient density, and near-zero industrially processed food.

eea_value.note: The 34% and 12% protein figures are model estimates (Eaton & Konner 1985, ext 39). Forager diets vary widely by habitat and season (Milton 2000, ext 763), and later reconstructions show wide ecological variation (Cordain et al. 2000, ext 729).

parameters.modern_default: A narrow, year-round-uniform diet built largely from a handful of refined commodity crops (wheat, corn, soy, sugar, refined oils) recombined into processed and ultra-processed products. Seasonality is erased by global supply chains; micronutrient density falls while energy density rises; near-total replacement of whole foods with industrially formulated ones.
parameters.gap_statement: The modern food environment collapses a seasonally varied, micronutrient-dense, whole-food omnivory into a year-round monotony of refined, energy-dense, nutrient-diluted products, removing both the variety and the whole-food matrix the metabolic and digestive systems were calibrated to.
parameters.resolution_unit: Whole-food matrix and dietary variety, not any single 'good' or 'bad' nutrient: the mismatch is in the wholesale shift to refined, processed forms across the whole diet, not in one macronutrient ratio.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (22 Nov 2026): tested many times that forager diets varied widely with habitat and drew less energy from carbohydrate than modern diets. Strongest: two independent analyses of the ethnographic codes for 229 forager societies, Cordain et al. 2000 (ext 729: animal foods above half of subsistence in 73% of societies, protein 19 to 35% of energy) and Ströhle and Hahn 2011 (ext 3616, 3617: carbohydrate from about 3 to 50% of energy, tracking latitude and habitat, below current recommendations in most societies). Main weakness: both rest on the same coarse codes of subsistence shares, skewed toward high-latitude groups, not measured intake. Change of diet with season is measured in single populations (Hadza: Marlowe and Berbesque 2009, ext 2687). Near-zero industrial processing follows from the period. Single figures such as 34% protein are model reconstructions (Eaton and Konner 1985, ext 39) and no single value holds.

parameters.name: Satiety-honest fiber and whole-food matrix (food that signals fullness truthfully)
parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral foods were fibrous, water- and bulk-rich, and slow to eat and digest, so the volume and macronutrient signals reaching satiety circuits tracked the actual caloric load. Reconstructions place ancestral fiber intake far above modern levels (on the order of 100 g/day or somewhat more vs ~20 g today; Eaton 2006, ext 3605). Sweetness, fat, and salt arrived bundled inside a whole-food matrix; sweet food was seasonal and costly to obtain (for the Hadza, honey is a favourite food and a substantial calorie share in season, Marlowe et al. 2014), and fat and salt came at concentrations that were ancestrally rare, so the reward-system's responses to those cues were honest proxies for nutritional value.

eea_value.note: Fiber figures are reconstructions (Eaton 2006, ext 3605, which lowered the 100 to 150 g of Eaton & Konner 1985, ext 39).
eea_value.sweet_fat_salt_availability: sweet food seasonal and costly (honey); fat and salt concentrations ancestrally rare; bundled in whole-food matrix

parameters.modern_default: Ultra-processed, hyperpalatable products engineered to the 'bliss point' - the mathematically optimized concentration of sugar, fat, and salt that maximizes craving - stripped of fiber and whole-food bulk. These foods decouple palatability from nutritional value and deliver calories faster than satiety signaling can register them, so the evolved fullness/reward proxies no longer track intake. Ultra-processed hyperpalatability is the modern proxy that defeats satiety.
parameters.gap_statement: Industrial formulation deliberately separates the reward cues (sweet/fat/salt) from the satiety cues (fiber, bulk, slow digestion) the two were ancestrally bundled together, so modern hyperpalatable food drives consumption past the point the body would otherwise stop, defeating the honest-signal logic of appetite regulation.
parameters.resolution_unit: Satiety-honesty of food (does palatability track nutritional/caloric load?), not calorie count alone: the failure is the engineered decoupling of reward from fullness, not merely high energy density.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade: argued, not yet tested. Journalism from industry documents and interviews records that food companies tune sugar, fat and salt to a 'bliss point' that maximizes craving (Moss 2013, ext 75, 76, 439, 440); those sources do not test whether this defeats satiety. In a two-week inpatient crossover trial, 20 adults ate 508 kcal a day more on an ultra-processed diet than on an unprocessed one matched for presented calories, sugar, sodium and fiber (Hall et al. 2019, ext 866). In a review of 185 prospective studies and 58 trials, the trials found lower bodyweight, systolic blood pressure and total cholesterol with more dietary fibre, and in the prospective studies the highest fibre intakes went with 15 to 30 percent less death from all causes and from cardiovascular disease, with the benefit greatest at 25 to 29 g a day and the dose-response curves pointing to more benefit at higher intakes (Reynolds et al. 2019). The ancestral fiber figure (about 100 g a day or somewhat more against 20 g today) is a model estimate (Eaton 2006, ext 3605), which lowered the 100 to 150 g of Eaton and Konner's 1985 model (ext 39). Hadza rank honey as their favourite food, and it supplies a substantial share of their calories (Marlowe et al. 2014, ext 730).

parameters.name: Acquisition effort (calories are physically worked for)
parameters.eea_baseline: Food had to be physically acquired: walked to, foraged, dug, hunted, and processed. Among the Hadza, GPS-measured daily walking distances average about 11.4 km for men and 5.8 km for women (Pontzer et al. 2012, 30 adults over 11 days) and, in a larger sample of 179 people over 2,078 person-days, 12.9 km for men and 7.6 km for women (Wood et al. 2021, ext 3418), and women also spend several hours digging; broader hunter-gatherer daily travel is on the order of ~10 km. This embeds substantial obligate movement and a real energetic and time cost between hunger and calories. Note: the absolute activity premium over sedentary moderns is modest (hunter-gatherer PAL ~1.8-1.9 vs ~1.6 for desk workers, ~15% higher), so the baseline is 'embedded all-day effort,' not extreme athleticism.

eea_value.note: Distances are GPS means for the Hadza (Pontzer et al. 2012). They are not work hours; for work hours see EEA-SUBS-04.
eea_value.hadza_distance_source: Pontzer et al. 2012, PLoS ONE, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0040503 (GPS, means; SD 2.1 men, 1.7 women); women also dig several hours (ext 196)

parameters.modern_default: Calories require essentially zero acquisition effort: hyperpalatable, energy-dense food is available on demand, pre-processed, often delivered, with no movement, foraging, or processing cost between impulse and ingestion. The effort gate that historically bounded intake is gone.
parameters.gap_statement: Removing the work between hunger and food eliminates a natural brake on consumption and decouples eating from the obligate daily movement it was bundled with - calories are now frictionless to obtain and detached from the physical activity that ancestrally accompanied acquisition.
parameters.resolution_unit: Incidental, embedded, all-day acquisition movement (walking, foraging, carrying, digging) - NOT 'exercise' as a discrete bout. The mismatch is the loss of effort woven through daily food-getting, not a missing gym session. Work hours: see EEA-SUBS-04.
parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Hadza daily distances are GPS-measured (Pontzer et al. 2012) and forager activity levels are compared across populations (Pontzer, Wood and Raichlen 2018); the distance figures are Hadza only.

evidence.author_quote: Among the many studies of the Hadza, one asked forty-six Hadza adults to wear lightweight heart rate monitors for several days. According to these sensors, the average adult Hadza spends a grand total of three hours and forty minutes a day doing light activities and two hours and fourteen minutes a day doing moderate or vigorous activities. Although these few hours of hustling and bustling per day make them about twelve times more active than the average American or European, by no stretch of the imagination could one characterize their workloads as backbreaking. On average, the women walk five miles a day and dig for several hours, whereas the men walk between seven and ten miles a day. And when they aren't being very active, they typically rest or do light work.
evidence.content: Lieberman reports a Hadza heart-rate monitor study of 46 adults: the average adult spent about 3 h 40 min a day in light activity and 2 h 14 min in moderate or vigorous activity, which he puts at about twelve times the activity of the average American or European, and he writes t

evidence.author_quote: Although there is much variation, PALs of hunter-gatherers average 1.9 for men and 1.8 for women, slightly below PAL scores for subsistence farmers, which average 2.1 for men and 1.9 for women. To put these values into context, hunter-gatherer PALs are about the same as those of factory workers and farmers in the developed world (1.8), and about 15 percent higher than PALs of people with desk jobs in developed countries (1.6). In other words, typical hunter-gatherers are about as physically active as Americans or Europeans who include about an hour of exercise in their daily routine. In case you are wondering, most mammals in the wild have PALs of 3.3 or more, nearly twice as high as hunter-gatherers. Thus, comparatively speaking, humans who must hunt and gather all the food they eat and make everything they own by hand are substantially less active than average free-ranging mammals.
